  • OID4VCI credential encryption: the issuer metadata advertises credential_request_encryption (driven by the ecdh-generated key in realm.defaultKeyProviders) and credential_response_encryption (RSA-OAEP via the realm's RSA key, not removable). Wallets that encrypt must put the kid in the request JWE header and must not send a top-level alg in credential_response_encryption. The EUDI reference wallet needs eudi-lib-ios-openid4vci-swift ≥ 0.40.0; Lissi does not encrypt and is unaffected. See release-notes/10-x.md → Credential request/response encryption (JWE) for the full details and error signatures.

docs.title: Complete example
docs.text: A complete working example with multiple credential types, users, and clients is available at k3s/consumer.yaml. This file is intended for local development and testing. For production deployments, replace test values (passwords, DIDs, domains) with your real configuration.

docs.title: Production considerations
docs.text:
• Use an external PostgreSQL instance with proper backups and high availability instead of the built-in managed PostgreSQL
  • Configure TLS for Keycloak's endpoints, and have the ingress refuse or redirect plain HTTP. The realm requires HTTPS for requests from public addresses (keycloak.realm.sslRequired: external, the default) and accepts plain HTTP from private ones, such as the components that call Keycloak inside the cluster. Keycloak takes the client address from the X-Forwarded-For header of the ingress (keycloak.keycloak.proxyHeaders: xforwarded), so it must not be reachable around the ingress, and it takes the scheme from the realm's frontendURL: with an https frontend URL, which wallets need anyway, it does not see a request that reached the ingress over HTTP, so that check is the ingress's. all requires HTTPS for internal calls too
  • Set strong admin credentials and rotate them regularly

docs.title: Cluster Prerequisites
docs.text:
What a Kubernetes cluster needs before any role of the FIWARE Data Space Connector is installed in it: the operators the charts rely on, the network the components expect, and the resources they use. It applies to every role - Consumer, Provider and Operator - and to the local marketplace.

The local deployment sets all of this up on its own, for a test environment on a single machine; this page is for clusters that are set up by hand.

  • Cluster Prerequisites
  • At a glance
  • Kubernetes
  • Databases
    • PostgreSQL deployed by the charts: the Zalando Postgres Operator
    • MongoDB deployed by the charts
    • Installing the operators once
  • cert-manager
  • Network
    • Public names have to resolve inside the cluster
    • Outbound access
    • Private CA
  • Sizing
    • Set memory limits on the Java components

docs.title: At a glance
docs.text: Requirement Needed Used by Kubernetes 1.26 or later (1.19 without the vc-operator) Always Every chart A default StorageClass When the charts deploy the databases, or other persistent components PostgreSQL, MongoDB, Vault An ingress controller (or a Gateway API implementation) and TLS certificates for the public hosts Always DID document, Keycloak, verifier, APISIX, marketplace, Trust Anchor PostgreSQL Always: an existing one, or one the charts deploy through the Zalando Postgres Operator All roles MongoDB With the local marketplace or the Trust Anchor's consent management: an existing one, or one the charts deploy through a MongoDB operator Provider, Operator cert-manager Optional, recommended Certificates of the public hosts and of the identity key Public names resolvable inside the cluster Always Verifier, APISIX, marketplace, vc-operator, Keycloak

docs.title: Kubernetes
docs.text:
• Version: the charts accept Kubernetes 1.19 or later, except the vc-operator, which needs 1.26. Use a Kubernetes release that is still supported upstream; the integration tests run on a current k3s.
  • Storage: the databases the charts deploy and, when enabled, Vault and APISIX's etcd request PersistentVolumeClaims from the default StorageClass unless their values name one, so the cluster needs a default StorageClass or a class set for each of them.
  • Ingress: the examples in these guides use Ingress resources with Traefik annotations; any ingress controller works, adapting the annotations. Every public host needs a TLS certificate from a CA the other participants trust.

docs.title: Databases
docs.text:
What the components need is the databases, not a particular way of running them:

  • PostgreSQL, for every role: Keycloak, the Trusted Issuers List, the verifier, the PAP and Scorpio in a connector, and the Trusted Issuers List in the Trust Anchor.
  • MongoDB, only for the local marketplace (Business API Ecosystem) and the Trust Anchor's consent management.

Each can be an existing database - a managed service such as Amazon RDS, Azure Database or Cloud SQL, or a deployment of your own - or one the charts deploy:

An existing database A database the charts deploy What the cluster needs Network access to it, and the databases and users created in it The operator that creates it: the Zalando Postgres Operator for PostgreSQL, a MongoDB operator for MongoDB Values The connection of each component, see Databases in the provider guide and Using an existing MongoDB for the marketplace. In the Trust Anchor, managedPostgres.enabled: false and trusted-issuers-list.database.* The default for PostgreSQL (managedPostgres); managedMongo for MongoDB

An existing PostgreSQL for a connector also needs the PostGIS extension in Scorpio's database.

docs.title: PostgreSQL deployed by the charts: the Zalando Postgres Operator
docs.text:
The databases the charts deploy are postgresql resources of the Zalando Postgres Operator, and both the connector and the Trust Anchor charts install that operator by default:

Chart Value that installs the operator Operator chart version data-space-connector decentralizedIam.vcAuthentication.postgres-operator.enabled 1.15.1 trust-anchor postgres-operator.enabled 1.15.1

The versions are the ones the charts on main depend on; check Chart.yaml (and Chart.lock) of the chart version you install.

An operator is cluster-wide: its CustomResourceDefinitions, ClusterRoles and webhooks exist once per cluster, and Helm lets only one release own them.

  • A single release in the cluster: keep the default.
  • More than one release in the cluster - a connector next to the Trust Anchor, or several connectors: install the operator once, on its own, and set those values to false in every release. A second release that installs it fails on the resources the first one owns.
  • No PostgreSQL deployed by the charts: set those values to false; the operator is not needed.

docs.title: MongoDB deployed by the charts
docs.text: managedMongo creates a MongoDBCommunity resource, handled by the MongoDB Community Operator or its successor, MongoDB Controllers for Kubernetes, which has to be installed beforehand. The connector chart can also install the Community Operator (mongo-operator.enabled, chart 0.13.0, off by default). Running a local marketplace explains how to install it.

docs.title: Installing the operators once
docs.text:
Install each operator the charts need with its upstream chart, in its own namespace, before any participant, and disable it in every participant's release:

helm repo add postgres-operator-charts https://opensource.zalando.com/postgres-operator/charts/postgres-operator
helm install postgres-operator postgres-operator-charts/postgres-operator \
  --version 1.15.1 --namespace postgres-operator --create-namespace

# in the values of every connector release
decentralizedIam:
  vcAuthentication:
    postgres-operator:
      enabled: false

# in the values of the trust-anchor release
postgres-operator:
  enabled: false

The local deployment follows the same pattern with the connector chart itself: k3s/operators.yaml installs the Postgres and MongoDB operators and cert-manager as a release of their own, with every other component disabled, and the participants' profiles turn them off. It is a test setup; in a production cluster, the upstream charts keep the operators' lifecycle independent of the connector's.

docs.title: cert-manager
docs.text:
cert-manager is not required, but the guides use it for the TLS certificates of the public hosts and for the identity key. The connector chart can install it (cert-manager.enabled, chart v1.21.2, off by default); like the operators, it can be installed only once per cluster.

Whatever issues the certificate that holds the DID's key has to keep that key on renewal: see Identity key lifecycle.

docs.title: Public names have to resolve inside the cluster
docs.text:
Several components call other components through their public HTTPS names, also when both run in the same cluster:

Component Calls Why VCVerifier The did:web of every credential issuer, and the Trust Anchor's TIR (tirAddress) To resolve the issuers' keys and check that they are trusted APISIX (openid-connect plugin) The verifier's discovery document and its jwks_uri To validate the access tokens; the discovery document announces the public jwks_uri even when discovery points inside the cluster Marketplace logic proxy The verifier's discovery document and token endpoint For the login, see Running a local marketplace vc-operator Keycloak's credential issuer To obtain the credentials it manages Keycloak The status list server, when statusListServer is enabled For the revocation status of the credentials it issues

From inside a pod those names have to reach the ingress, not something else. In a cluster behind a cloud load balancer they usually do: the name resolves to the load balancer's public address and the traffic comes back in (hairpin NAT). Check it, because some load balancers and most local or on-premises setups do not route traffic from the cluster back to its own public address. The alternatives:

  • Split-horizon DNS: the organization's internal DNS, used by the nodes, resolves the public names to the ingress' internal address.
  • A CoreDNS rewrite: the cluster DNS answers the public names with the ingress controller's Service. In k3s and RKE2, CoreDNS imports the coredns-custom ConfigMap, which leaves the CoreDNS configuration the distribution manages untouched:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: coredns-custom
  namespace: kube-system
data:
  # resolve every name under <your_domain> to the ingress controller's Service
  public-names.override: |
    rewrite stop {
      name regex (.+)\.<your_domain_regex>\.$ <ingress_service>.<ingress_namespace>.svc.cluster.local.
      answer auto
    }

<your_domain_regex> is the domain with its dots escaped (example\.org), and <ingress_service>.<ingress_namespace> the Service of the ingress controller, for example ingress-nginx-controller.ingress-nginx. Managed clusters have their own way to extend the cluster DNS (EKS, GKE, AKS).

To check it, resolve and call a public name from a pod in the connector's namespace:

kubectl -n <your_namespace> run dns-check --rm -it --restart=Never --image=curlimages/curl -- \
  curl -sS https://<your_did_domain>/.well-known/did.json

docs.title: Outbound access
docs.text:
Besides the other participants' public names (their DIDs, the Trust Anchor's TIR, and a Central Marketplace if there is one), the cluster needs to reach:

  • the image registries: quay.io, docker.io and ghcr.io, plus those of the operators' images;
  • Maven Central (repo1.maven.org), when Keycloak loads the token status list plugin with the chart's helper: an init container downloads it on every start. keycloak.tokenStatusList.plugin.mavenBaseUrl can point to a mirror;
  • the JSON-LD contexts the credentials reference (such as https://www.w3.org/2018/credentials/v1), for the verifier.

If outbound traffic goes through a proxy, give HTTPS_PROXY to the components that call out - the verifier's deployment.additionalEnvVars, Keycloak's proxy.*, the marketplace's and the vc-operator's environment, and proxy_opts in APISIX's openid-connect plugin - and keep the in-cluster services out of it with NO_PROXY (.svc, .cluster.local, and the Service names the component calls, such as trusted-issuers-list and credentials-config-service for the verifier).

docs.title: Private CA
docs.text:
If the public hosts have certificates from a private CA, every component that calls them has to trust it. Never turn the verification off instead.

Component How to trust the CA APISIX apisix.ssl.existingCASecret, see Trusting a private CA VCVerifier An init container that appends the CA to the image's bundle (/etc/ssl/cert.pem) in a shared volume mounted over it, as k3s/provider.yaml does. The chart's serverCertificates.caCert only takes effect when other init containers are configured too Marketplace logic proxy NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS, see Running a local marketplace vc-operator SSL_CERT_FILE pointing to the CA, mounted with extraVolumes/extraVolumeMounts, as in k3s/provider.yaml. Keycloak tls.truststoreEnabled with a Java truststore in tls.truststoreExistingSecret Contract Management No option to add a CA: the hosts it calls (the Central Marketplace) need a certificate from a public CA

docs.title: Sizing
docs.text:
The figures below were measured with chart 10.13.2 (trust-anchor 1.3.0) and the local deployment's profiles (k3s/), one release per role on a single k3s node, after the components had settled and without load. They give the floor a role needs, not its capacity: plan the headroom for your traffic on top of them.

Role Memory in use CPU in use Images (compressed) Disk for images Trust Anchor (TIR/TIL and PostgreSQL) 0.3 GiB 0.02 cores 0.8 GB ~2.5 GB Consumer (Keycloak, DID, PostgreSQL) 0.8 GiB 0.05 cores 1.0 GB ~3 GB Provider without the marketplace 2.3 GiB 0.2 cores 2.2 GB ~7 GB Provider with the local marketplace 2.6 GiB 0.25 cores 4.2 GB ~13 GB Operators (Postgres, MongoDB, cert-manager) 0.1 GiB 0.01 cores 0.15 GB ~0.5 GB
  • Memory: the largest consumers at rest are Keycloak (~0.6 GiB), Scorpio (~0.4 GiB), the TM Forum API (~0.35 GiB), PostgreSQL (~0.2 GiB per cluster), the Trusted Issuers List and contract-management (~0.2 GiB each) and APISIX (~0.2 GiB). The verifier, the PAP, OPA and did-helper use a few tens of MiB.
  • Disk: the container runtime keeps both the downloaded and the unpacked layers, about three times the compressed size of the images, on every node that runs them. Add the PersistentVolumes: by default 1 GiB for each PostgreSQL cluster and 1 GiB + 1 GiB for the marketplace's MongoDB, which hold a few hundred MiB on a fresh installation.
  • CPU: at rest, a fraction of a core per role. Startup needs more, mostly for the Java components (Keycloak, Scorpio, the TM Forum API, the Trusted Issuers List, contract-management).

docs.title: Set memory limits on the Java components
docs.text:
Most components declare no resources by default, so the scheduler reserves nothing for them and nothing bounds them. That matters most for the Java components: without a memory limit, the JVM sizes its heap from the memory of the node, not from what the component needs. On a long-running installation with 64 GiB nodes and no limits, Scorpio grew to ~17 GiB and the TM Forum API to ~8.5 GiB, against the ~0.4 GiB they use after a fresh start.

Give every component requests and limits through its chart's resources - in particular Scorpio, the TM Forum API, the Trusted Issuers List and contract-management - and size the limits with your own measurements under load (kubectl top pods --containers). The PostgreSQL clusters take their resources from the operator's defaults (100m CPU and 100 MiB requested, 1 CPU and 500 MiB limit) unless resources is set in decentralizedIam.vcAuthentication.managedPostgres.config (in the trust-anchor chart, managedPostgres.config), which is the postgresql resource's spec; 500 MiB is little for a database that several components share.

docs.title: Consumer Role
docs.text:
Note

This guide covers the deployment of an organization acting exclusively as a consumer. If your organization also needs to act as a provider (offering data or services to other participants), refer to the Consumer & Provider guide instead.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: A Consumer is an organization that retrieves data or services from other participants in the data space. The consumer does not host data services itself — it only needs the ability to authenticate its users and issue Verifiable Credentials that can be presented to providers.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
Before deploying, contact the Data Space Operator to initiate the onboarding process for your organization. The Operator will guide you through:

  • The documentation and requirements needed to join the data space
  • Registration of your organization's DID at the Trust Anchor
  • The credential types your organization is allowed to issue and their required configuration (claims, attribute mappings, etc.)
  • The Trust Anchor's TIR endpoint URL

This information is needed to configure Keycloak, the DID, and the Verifiable Credentials correctly.

Check also that the cluster meets the Cluster Prerequisites: its databases, the network requirements and the resources the consumer needs.

docs.title: Verifiable Credential Issuer
docs.text:
A consumer organization requires a Verifiable Credential (VC) Issuer, a component capable of issuing Verifiable Credentials to its users so they can authenticate and access services offered by providers in the data space.

The FIWARE Data Space Connector uses Keycloak as the VC issuer. For detailed configuration instructions, see the Keycloak Configuration guide.

docs.title: Database
docs.text: Keycloak stores its data in PostgreSQL: an existing one, or one the chart deploys with decentralizedIam.vcAuthentication.managedPostgres. See Databases in the provider guide for both options.

docs.title: DID
docs.text:
Every participant in the data space needs a Decentralized Identifier (DID), a globally unique identifier that the organization controls and that is not dependent on a centralized registry. DIDs can be of different types (methods), such as did:key, did:web, did:ebsi, among others.

  • did:web — Recommended for production environments. It relies on a domain name controlled by the organization and serves the DID document over HTTPS, providing discoverability and a natural trust anchor tied to DNS.
  • did:key — Suitable only for test or development environments. It encodes the public key directly in the identifier itself, which makes it simple to generate but offers no discoverability or key rotation capabilities.

The DID Helper is a lightweight service that creates did:key or serves the consumer's DID document.

Note

If the data space uses the Decentralized Claims Protocol (DCP) (typically together with the Dataspace Protocol via FDSC-EDC), the DID Helper is replaced by the Identity Hub, which serves the DID document (and the consumer's credentials) as required by DCP. See the Dataspace Protocol Integration Guide for details.

The DID document contains the consumer's public key, which providers use to verify that credentials were issued by this organization. The DID must be registered at the data space's Trust Anchor following the Data Space onboarding process.

docs.title: Dataspace Protocol(FDSC-EDC and IdentityHub)
docs.text:
If the data space requires compliance with the Dataspace Protocol (DSP), the consumer can enable the Eclipse Dataspace Components connector. This adds support for standardized contract negotiation and data transfer protocols.

Enable this when: - The data space mandates DSP compliance - You need to interact with non-FIWARE DSP-compliant connectors - Contract negotiation must follow the IDSA protocol

See DSP Integration for configuration details.

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text:
The consumer role does not require deploying a FIWARE DSC, since it only needs a DID and a VC issuer (Keycloak), and that is not a FIWARE Data Space Connector.

However, for easier deployment of these components, you can use the same fiware/data-space-connector Helm chart as the provider, but with most components disabled. You only need to enable Keycloak and the DID Helper as mandatory components. If you prefer not to use the FIWARE DSC Helm chart, you can always deploy these components separately using their own Helm charts or deployment methods.

docs.title: Using the FIWARE DSC Helm chart and values
docs.text:
Start from the reference profile

examples/consumer.yaml is a complete values file for a consumer, to adapt to your installation. Its README lists the prerequisites, the placeholders, the Secrets to create and the installation steps. The settings below explain each part.

Build a values.yaml for the consumer by adapting examples/consumer.yaml. It uses the same fiware/data-space-connector chart as the provider, but with most components disabled: a consumer only issues credentials to its users. The sections below show that file piece by piece; replace every <placeholder>.

The ingresses use cert-manager through annotations and the ingress class you set (the local deployment uses Traefik). A ClusterIssuer is a prerequisite: use your own, or let the chart create one with certManagerResources (the examples README covers the prerequisites, Secrets and placeholders).

docs.title: Identity: did:web
docs.text:
did-helper serves the organization's did:web. Its key is the TLS certificate cert-manager issues for the ingress, and it must never rotate: a new key changes the DID, and every credential issued with the old one stops verifying (hence private-key-rotation-policy: Never; see Identity key lifecycle in the provider guide, which applies to consumers too).

did:
  enabled: true
  config:
    server:
      # did-helper also publishes <hostUrl>/.well-known/tls.crt, the certificate of the key
      hostUrl: https://<did-domain>
      certPath: /certs/tls.crt
  volumes:
    - name: certs
      secret:
        # the DID's key: the certificate cert-manager issues for the ingress below
        secretName: did-tls
        items:
          - key: tls.crt
            path: tls.crt
  volumeMounts:
    - name: certs
      mountPath: /certs
  # with certPath did-helper writes nothing, so it runs on a read-only root filesystem
  securityContext:
    readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
    allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
    capabilities:
      drop: ["ALL"]
  ingress:
    enabled: true
    className: <ingress-class>
    annotations:
      cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: <cluster-issuer>
      cert-manager.io/private-key-algorithm: ECDSA
      # the Secret also holds the DID's key: a renewal must keep it, or the DID changes and every
      # credential issued with the old key stops verifying
      cert-manager.io/private-key-rotation-policy: Never
    hosts:
      - host: <did-domain>
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: ImplementationSpecific
    tls:
      - secretName: did-tls
        hosts:
          - <did-domain>

docs.title: Credential issuer: Keycloak
docs.text:
Keycloak issues the consumer's users their credentials and signs them with the DID's key: the prepare-keystore init container turns the DID Secret into the PKCS12 keystore the realm reads. The ingress publishes only /realms/<realm> and /resources; the admin console and the master realm stay inside the cluster. See Keycloak configuration.

keycloak:
  enabled: true
  keycloak:
    # the public URL, so that Keycloak does not derive it from each request
    hostname: https://<keycloak-domain>
    hostnameStrict: true
  # its own database user, created by the Postgres operator (see managedPostgres below)
  database:
    username: keycloak
    existingSecret: keycloak.postgres.credentials.postgresql.acid.zalan.do
  ingress:
    enabled: true
    className: <ingress-class>
    annotations:
      cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: <cluster-issuer>
      cert-manager.io/private-key-algorithm: ECDSA
    hosts:
      - host: <keycloak-domain>
        paths:
          # only what wallets need: the realm's endpoints and the static resources. The admin
          # console and the master realm stay inside the cluster (kubectl port-forward).
          - path: /realms/<realm>
            pathType: Prefix
          - path: /resources
            pathType: Prefix
    tls:
      - secretName: keycloak-tls
        hosts:
          - <keycloak-domain>
  # Keycloak signs the credentials with the DID's key: this init container turns the key and
  # certificate of the DID's Secret into the PKCS12 keystore the realm reads
  extraInitContainers:
    - name: prepare-keystore
      image: alpine/openssl:3.5.5
      command: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]
      args:
        - |
          # the CA of the certificate goes into the keystore too, when the Secret has it (a
          # private CA); a public one, such as Let's Encrypt, leaves ca.crt out or empty
          ca=""
          if [ -s /certs-did/ca.crt ]; then ca="-certfile /certs-did/ca.crt"; fi
          openssl pkcs12 -export \
            -in /certs-did/tls.crt \
            -inkey /certs-did/tls.key \
            $ca \
            -out /did-material/cert.pfx \
            -name "didPrivateKey" \
            -passout env:STORE_PASS
          chmod 644 /did-material/cert.pfx
      env:
        - name: STORE_PASS
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: keystore-password
              key: password
      volumeMounts:
        - name: did-material
          mountPath: /did-material
        - name: did-key
          mountPath: /certs-did
          readOnly: true
  extraVolumeMounts:
    # Keycloak only reads realm keystores from /opt/keycloak/data/<realm name>
    - name: did-material
      mountPath: /opt/keycloak/data/<realm>
    - name: realms
      mountPath: /opt/keycloak/data/import
  extraVolumes:
    - name: did-material
      emptyDir: {}
    # the realm the chart renders, in the ConfigMap <realm name>-realm
    - name: realms
      configMap:
        name: <realm>-realm
    - name: did-key
      secret:
        secretName: did-tls
  # replaces the chart's list: keep KC_HEAP_SIZE
  extraEnvVars:
    - name: KC_HEAP_SIZE
      value: "1024m"
    - name: STORE_PASS
      valueFrom:
        secretKeyRef:
          name: keystore-password
          key: password
  issuerDid: <did>
  signingKey:
    storePath: /opt/keycloak/data/<realm>/cert.pfx
    storePassword: "${STORE_PASS}"
    keyAlias: didPrivateKey
    keyPassword: "${STORE_PASS}"
    did: <did>
    keyAlgorithm: ES256
  realm:
    name: <realm>
    frontendUrl: https://<keycloak-domain>
    import: true
    # One credential type: UserCredential, carrying the user's name, e-mail and the roles the
    # user holds at the provider below. Add one entry per credential type your data space uses.
    verifiableCredentials:
      user-credential:
        attributes:
          format: jwt_vc_json
          verifiable_credential_type: UserCredential
          credential_signing_alg: ES256
          credential_build_config.token_jws_type: JWT
        protocolMappers:
          - name: context-mapper
            protocol: oid4vc
            protocolMapper: oid4vc-context-mapper
            config:
              context: https://www.w3.org/2018/credentials/v1
          - name: email-mapper
            protocol: oid4vc
            protocolMapper: oid4vc-user-attribute-mapper
            config:
              claim.name: email
              userAttribute: email
          - name: firstName-mapper
            protocol: oid4vc
            protocolMapper: oid4vc-user-attribute-mapper
            config:
              claim.name: firstName
              userAttribute: firstName
          - name: lastName-mapper
            protocol: oid4vc
            protocolMapper: oid4vc-user-attribute-mapper
            config:
              claim.name: lastName
              userAttribute: lastName
          # the roles of the user at the provider, read from the client named after its DID
          - name: provider-roles-mapper
            protocol: oid4vc
            protocolMapper: oid4vc-target-role-mapper
            config:
              claim.name: roles
              clientId: <provider-did>
          - name: subject-id-mapper
            protocol: oid4vc
            protocolMapper: oid4vc-subject-id-mapper
            config:
              userAttribute: email
              claim.name: id
    # Roles a user can hold at the provider. Their names have to match the provider's access
    # policies. Users are not part of the values: create them in the realm, or federate it.
    clientRoles: |
      "<provider-did>": [
        {
          "name": "READER",
          "description": "Is allowed to read the provider's data",
          "clientRole": true
        }
      ]
    # the client the roles above belong to, named after the DID. It only holds roles: no login
    # flow is enabled on it.
    clients: |
      {
        "clientId": "<provider-did>",
        "description": "Roles of the users at the provider",
        "enabled": true,
        "protocol": "openid-connect",
        "publicClient": false,
        "standardFlowEnabled": false,
        "implicitFlowEnabled": false,
        "directAccessGrantsEnabled": false,
        "serviceAccountsEnabled": false
      }

docs.title: Database
docs.text:
A consumer only runs Keycloak's database. The chart's managed PostgreSQL creates its user, with the Postgres operator installed once per cluster; the verifier, trusted issuers list and policy components stay off.

decentralizedIam:
  enabled: true
  vcAuthentication:
    # the Postgres operator is installed once per cluster, not by each release
    postgres-operator:
      enabled: false
    # Keycloak's database. The operator creates its user and the Secret with the password. (The
    # chart also creates the databases of the components a consumer does not run; they stay empty.)
    managedPostgres:
      enabled: true
      config:
        volume:
          size: 5Gi
          # storageClass: <storage-class>
    vcverifier:
      enabled: false
    credentials-config-service:
      enabled: false
    trusted-issuers-list:
      enabled: false
  odrlAuthorization:
    odrl-pap:
      enabled: false
    apisix:
      enabled: false

docs.title: Disabled components
docs.text:
The data and contract components a consumer does not run are set to false.

scorpio:
  enabled: false
tm-forum-api:
  enabled: false
contract-management:
  enabled: false

docs.title: Install the chart
docs.text:
Install the chart with your values, pinning its version (see the release notes for what changes between versions):

helm install consumer oci://quay.io/fiware/helm-charts/data-space-connector \
  --version <version> \
  -n consumer \
  --create-namespace \
  -f consumer-values.yaml

The chart is also available from the Helm repository https://fiware.github.io/data-space-connector:

helm repo add fiware-dsc https://fiware.github.io/data-space-connector
helm install consumer fiware-dsc/data-space-connector --version <version> -n consumer --create-namespace -f consumer-values.yaml

docs.title: Other deployment options
docs.text:
A base example for a consumer deployment can be found at k3s/consumer.yaml.

Note

These values are intended for local development and testing environments. For a real production deployment, they must be customized to meet your infrastructure, security, and availability requirements. See Production considerations below.

For other deployment scenarios, the base consumer.yaml can be extended with additional overlay values files (which take precedence over the base). The following overlays are available:

Overlay File Description eIDAS / ELSI k3s/consumer-eidas.yaml Configuration for deployments compliant with the ELSI trust framework, including eIDAS certificate issuance via Keycloak. See eIDAS 2.0 Compliance for details Gaia-X k3s/consumer-gaia-x.yaml Configuration for Gaia-X compliant deployments TM Forum APIs k3s/consumer-tmf.yaml Enables TM Forum APIs on the consumer (required for central marketplace and EDC-related features) Auth components k3s/consumer-auth.yaml Configures authentication components for the consumer (required for central marketplace and EDC-related features) DSP k3s/dsp-consumer.yaml Enables the Dataspace Protocol (DSP) connector on the consumer side

For example, to deploy a consumer with DSP support and TM Forum APIs:

helm install consumer oci://quay.io/fiware/helm-charts/data-space-connector --version <version> \
  -n consumer \
  -f k3s/consumer.yaml \
  -f k3s/consumer-auth.yaml \
  -f k3s/consumer-tmf.yaml \
  -f k3s/dsp-consumer.yaml

docs.title: TLS certificates
docs.text:
• All publicly reachable endpoints must use HTTPS with valid TLS certificates issued by a trusted CA
  • You can enable cert-manager directly in the FIWARE DSC Helm chart to automate certificate issuance and renewal

docs.title: DID and key management
docs.text:
• Use a registered domain name that your organization controls for the did:web identifier
  • Ensure the DID document is served over HTTPS with a valid certificate
  • Protect the private key associated with your DID: it is the foundation of your organization's identity in the data space. If compromised, an attacker could issue credentials on your behalf
  • Give the DID a dedicated key that renewals do not regenerate, not the TLS Secret of an Ingress: see Identity key lifecycle in the provider guide, which applies to consumers as well

docs.title: Trust Anchor registration
docs.text:
• Register your organization's DID at the data space's Trust Anchor before deploying
  • Coordinate with the Data Space Operator regarding:
  • The Trust Anchor's TIR endpoint URL (needed for provider credential verification)

docs.title: Credential configuration
docs.text:
• Configure only the credential types that your organization actually needs to issue
  • Define appropriate claims and attribute mappings for each credential type
  • Set reasonable credential expiry times
  • Review credential scopes to ensure they follow the principle of least privilege

docs.title: Keycloak
docs.text:
• Do not hardcode passwords in values files; use Kubernetes Secrets
  • Rotate Keycloak admin credentials and the keystore password regularly
  • For high availability, deploy at least 2 replicas with Infinispan cache replication enabled

docs.title: Upgrade strategy
docs.text:
• Review the FIWARE Data Space Connector release notes before each upgrade for breaking changes
  • Keep the connector version aligned across all participants in the data space when possible to avoid protocol incompatibilities

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
In most real-world data spaces, organizations act as both consumer and provider simultaneously. They offer their own data or services to the data space while also consuming data from other participants. This is the most common deployment scenario.

Important

To deploy as both consumer and provider, you must follow both the Consumer guide and the Provider guide. Each guide covers the components, configuration, and deployment steps for its respective role. This document only provides additional recommendations specific to the combined scenario.

docs.title: Do not duplicate DID and Keycloak
docs.text:
An organization has a single identity in the data space, regardless of how many roles it plays. When deploying as both consumer and provider:

  • One DID — The Decentralized Identifier is unique per organization. Do not create separate DIDs for the consumer and provider functions.
  • One Keycloak instance — A single Keycloak instance issues Verifiable Credentials for both roles: credentials that your users present to other providers (consumer function) and credentials for your own employees/services (provider function). The same realm handles both.

docs.title: Evolving from one role to the other
docs.text:
• Consumer to provider — If your organization initially deploys as a consumer only and later needs to become a provider, you can add the provider components (VCVerifier, Trusted Issuers List, APISIX, OPA, ODRL-PAP, etc.) to the existing deployment. The DID and Keycloak are already in place.
  • Provider to consumer — If your organization already has a FIWARE Data Space Connector deployed as a provider, it already includes all the components needed to act as a consumer (Keycloak and DID). You only need to configure the Keycloak realm with the appropriate clients, roles, and credential types for the target providers.

docs.title: Production considerations
docs.text: All production considerations from both the Consumer and Provider guides apply. Additionally:

docs.title: Shared components
docs.text: With a single deployment, a failure in shared components (PostgreSQL, Keycloak) affects both consumer and provider functions. Consider deploying Keycloak and PostgreSQL with high availability to mitigate this risk.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Data Space Operator runs the shared trust infrastructure of the data space. It does not take part in data exchange the way a consumer or provider does; it is the neutral authority that maintains the trust framework so participants can interact securely.

In a FIWARE Data Space, the Operator's main responsibility is running the Trust Anchor: the central registry where all trusted participants and their credentials are registered.

The cluster that runs the Trust Anchor needs the Cluster Prerequisites, in particular, when the chart deploys its PostgreSQL, a single installation of the Postgres operator per cluster.

docs.title: Participant onboarding
docs.text:
The Operator is also responsible for onboarding new organizations into the data space. This involves validating the required documentation and registering the organization in the Trust Anchor.

  1. Verify the organization's identity and legitimacy (out-of-band process)
  2. Register the organization's DID at the Trust Anchor
  3. Define which credential types the organization is allowed to issue
  4. Communicate the Trust Anchor's TIR endpoint to the new participant

To support this task, an Onboarding Portal is available as an optional component.

docs.title: Trusted Issuers Registry (TIR)
docs.text:
The Trusted Issuers Registry implements the EBSI Trusted Issuers Registry API, providing a standardized way to query which organizations are trusted in the data space.

  • Exposes a read-only API (/v4/issuers) for participants to verify trust
  • Backed by a management API (/issuer) for registering and managing trusted issuers

Note

The FIWARE Trusted Issuers Registry is the default implementation shipped with the FIWARE Data Space Connector, but it is not the only option. Any component that exposes the EBSI Trusted Issuers Registry API can serve as the Trust Anchor's registry, including blockchain-backed implementations such as the EBSI Trusted Issuers Registry itself. A data space can then match the trust registry to its own governance and decentralization model.

docs.title: Trusted Issuers List (TIL) management API
docs.text: The management interface allows the Operator to: - Register new participants (by their DID) as trusted issuers - Define which credential types each issuer is allowed to issue - Remove participants that are no longer trusted

docs.title: Database (SQL)
docs.text:
The Trust Anchor requires an SQL database to persist the list of trusted issuers.

The Trust Anchor must have its own dedicated database instance, separate from any participant's infrastructure. Because the Operator is neutral and independent of any provider or consumer, sharing a database would compromise the neutrality and security of the trust registry.

docs.title: Onboarding Portal
docs.text:
The Onboarding Portal is a web application that streamlines the process of onboarding new organizations into the data space. It provides a user interface for:

  • Submitting and reviewing the documentation required to join the data space
  • Validating the organization's identity and DID
  • Registering the organization in the Trust Anchor upon approval

The Onboarding Portal simplifies the Operator's work by replacing manual registration processes with a guided workflow. See the Onboarding Portal documentation for deployment and configuration details.

docs.title: Central Marketplace
docs.text:
Some data spaces run a shared Central Marketplace where providers publish offerings and consumers browse and purchase access. In a neutral governance model, the Operator is the natural host for such a marketplace, since it is already the non-participant entity trusted by every organization in the data space.

Note

The Central Marketplace is not a Provider. It does not host data services or protect them with a PAP; it only provides a catalog, an ordering API and a UI. Its role is to broker purchases and notify the actual data providers so they can enforce access on their own infrastructure.

Hosting the Central Marketplace is optional and independent from operating the Trust Anchor. Both responsibilities can sit with the same actor or be split between different ones. Either way, the Central Marketplace must be deployed with its own DID, its own database and its own Kubernetes namespace, and must not share infrastructure with the Trust Anchor's TIR.

docs.title: Required components
docs.text:
The Central Marketplace is deployed using the same fiware/data-space-connector Helm chart as a Provider, but with a specific subset of components enabled:

Component Purpose Keycloak Issues the credential used by the marketplace to authenticate against each provider's Contract Management when sending order notifications. Uses its own realm and did:web. In this documentation and in the shipped examples this credential is a MarketplaceCredential, but the credential type is not fixed — any type can be used as long as the marketplace's Keycloak issues it and the providers accept it (see Authentication credential type). DID Helper Publishes the marketplace's DID document. TMForum API Hosts the shared catalog (products, offerings, orders, parties, agreements). All interactions with the marketplace (organization registration, product specification, offering, ordering and order completion) can be performed directly through this API — see the end-to-end flow in CENTRAL_MARKETPLACE.md. Scorpio Context Broker NGSI-LD backend for the TMForum API. Should not be exposed to participants as a data service. Contract Management Configured in central-marketplace mode: enableCentralMarketplace: true, enableOdrlPap: false, oid4vp.enabled: true. On order completion, it authenticates with the marketplace's credential and notifies the provider's Contract Management. VCVerifier + Trusted Issuers List (local) Authenticate the providers (and users) that access the marketplace's catalog and ordering APIs.

The ODRL-PAP, OPA and data-service protection components that a Provider deploys are not needed in the Central Marketplace, because it does not expose protected data services.

docs.title: Optional components
docs.text:
Component Purpose Marketplace UI (BAE) Business API Ecosystem web portal (Logic Proxy + Charging Backend + APIs) on top of the TMForum API. Offers a user-friendly interface for participants to register, publish offerings and purchase access — all the same actions that can be performed directly through the TMForum APIs. Requires BAE_LP_DATASPACE_ENABLED=true and BAE_LP_PURCHASE_ENABLED=true for data space purchase flows, plus its own MongoDB.

Note

The Marketplace UI is not strictly required for the Central Marketplace to be operational — a headless deployment (TMForum API + Contract Management only) is valid, and all the flows documented in CENTRAL_MARKETPLACE.md can be driven exclusively through the TMForum APIs. However, for production deployments it is highly recommended to deploy the UI, since it provides a usable experience for end-users (sellers publishing offerings, customers browsing and buying). A UI-less deployment is a reasonable choice only when the scenario is purely machine-to-machine and participants integrate directly with the TMForum APIs from their own systems.

docs.title: Database
docs.text:
The Central Marketplace requires its own dedicated SQL database, separate from the Trust Anchor's database. It holds the Keycloak realm, the TMForum catalog (products, offerings, orders, agreements) and the Contract Management state (notifications, retries).

If the Marketplace UI (BAE) is also deployed, its Charging Backend additionally requires a MongoDB instance (used for the BAE user profiles and purchases). MongoDB can be deployed alongside the chart using the MongoDB Community Operator via mongo-operator.enabled: true and managedMongo.enabled: true. If the UI is not deployed, MongoDB is not needed.

docs.title: Deployment values
docs.text:
The Central Marketplace uses the fiware/data-space-connector Helm chart with a different subset of components enabled than a Provider. The snippets below show the key values required on top of a standard deployment — the full list of components (ingresses, TLS, Keycloak realm, credential definitions, etc.) follows the same patterns documented for the Provider role. See also the local demo overlays in k3s/consumer.yaml, k3s/consumer-auth.yaml and k3s/consumer-tmf.yaml for a complete example.

1. Enable Contract Management in central-marketplace mode

This is the component that reacts to order completions in the marketplace and sends notifications to the provider's Contract Management authenticating with the marketplace's credential.

contract-management:
  enabled: true
  did: <marketplace-DID>                    # e.g. did:web:did-central-marketplace.example.org
  enableCentralMarketplace: true            # drive the flow from marketplace orders, not from local ones
  enableOdrlPap: false                      # the marketplace does not run a local PAP
  enableTrustedIssuersList: false           # the marketplace does not manage a TIL for participants
  organization:
    provider:
      role: seller                          # see note below
  oid4vp:
    enabled: true                           # authenticate against providers using the marketplace's credential
    credentialsFolder: /credential-repo
    holder:
      holderId: <marketplace-DID>
      keyType: EC
      keyPath: /app/resources/signing-key/tls.key
      signatureAlgorithm: ECDH-ES
  services:
    product-order:    { url: http://tm-forum-api-svc:8080 }
    party:            { url: http://tm-forum-api-svc:8080 }
    product-catalog:  { url: http://tm-forum-api-svc:8080 }
    service-catalog:  { url: http://tm-forum-api-svc:8080 }
    tmforum-agreement-api: { url: http://tm-forum-api-svc:8080 }
    quote:            { url: http://tm-forum-api-svc:8080 }
  notification:
    enabled: true
    host: contract-management
  deployment:
    image:
      tag: 3.3.8                            # minimum image required for central marketplace mode

When a TMForum ProductOrder is completed, Contract Management inspects the relatedParty list of the underlying ProductSpecification to determine which participant is the provider, and therefore which Contract Management it must send the activation notification to. organization.provider.role configures the relatedParty.role value that Contract Management looks for. The chart default is provider, which matches the value written by clients that call the TMForum API directly (as in the demo flow). When the Marketplace UI (BAE) is deployed instead, it tags the provider with the role seller, so in that case this value must be overridden to seller. If the configured value does not match the role that clients write into relatedParty, Contract Management will not be able to resolve the provider from the order and no notification will be sent.

2. Enable the TMForum API and its NGSI-LD backend

The TMForum API hosts the shared catalog, orders and parties. It runs in allInOne mode on top of a Scorpio Context Broker that is not exposed publicly.

tm-forum-api:
  enabled: true
  allInOne:
    enabled: true
  defaultConfig:
    ngsiLd:
      url: http://data-service-scorpio:9090

scorpio:
  enabled: true
  fullnameOverride: data-service-scorpio
  ingress:
    enabled: false                          # NGSI-LD backend must not be publicly reachable

3. (Optional) Enable the Marketplace UI (BAE)

The Marketplace UI is an optional component: it is not required for the Central Marketplace to work, but highly recommended in production so that end-users get a usable web interface. For purely machine-to-machine scenarios, this whole block can be omitted and participants can interact directly with the TMForum API.

The Business API Ecosystem is the web portal that participants use to publish offerings and purchase access. The Logic Proxy must be started with the data-space flags so SIOP login and purchase flows are enabled.

marketplace:
  enabled: true
  externalUrl: https://<marketplace-domain>
  siop:
    clientId: <marketplace-DID>
    verifier:
      host: https://<verifier-domain>
      qrCodePath: /api/v2/loginQR
      tokenPath: /token
      jwksPath: /.well-known/jwks
    allowedRoles: [seller, customer, admin]
  tmForum:
    catalog:     { host: tm-forum-api-svc, port: 8080, path: /tmf-api/productCatalogManagement/v4 }
    inventory:   { host: tm-forum-api-svc, port: 8080, path: /tmf-api/productInventory/v4 }
    ordering:    { host: tm-forum-api-svc, port: 8080, path: /tmf-api/productOrderingManagement/v4 }
    party:       { host: tm-forum-api-svc, port: 8080, path: /tmf-api/party/v4 }
    # ... other TMForum sub-APIs (billing, usage, customer, resources, services, ...)
  bizEcosystemLogicProxy:
    ingress:
      enabled: true
      hosts:
        - host: <marketplace-domain>
          paths: ["/"]
      tls:
        - secretName: <marketplace-domain>-tls
          hosts: [<marketplace-domain>]
    additionalEnvVars:
      - { name: BAE_LP_SIOP_IS_REDIRECTION, value: "true" }
      - { name: BAE_LP_PURCHASE_ENABLED,     value: "true" }
      - { name: BAE_LP_DATASPACE_ENABLED,    value: "true" }
      - { name: BAE_LP_DSP_ENABLED,          value: "true" }
      - { name: BAE_LP_SIOP_PRIVATE_KEY_PEM, value: /certs-did/tls.key }
      - { name: BAE_LP_BILLING_ENGINE_URL,   value: "http://<release>-biz-ecosystem-charging-backend.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local:8006/charging/api/orderManagement/orders/preview/" }

When this block is enabled, remember to also override contract-management.organization.provider.role to seller (see step 1), since BAE tags the provider with that role in the ProductSpecification's relatedParty.

BAE_LP_DSP_ENABLED=true is optional and only required when providers must be able to create DSP-compatible product specifications and offerings (i.e. offerings whose data is exchanged over the Dataspace Protocol) through the Marketplace UI. It exposes the DSP-specific fields in the offering-creation forms. Omit it for a marketplace that only brokers classic FIWARE offerings. See Using the BAE Marketplace in the DSP Integration documentation.

4. Issue the marketplace's authentication credential from Keycloak

The Contract Management sends the notifications authenticated with a Verifiable Credential issued by the marketplace's own Keycloak. In this documentation and in the shipped examples this credential is a MarketplaceCredential, defined in the realm as the marketplace-credential entry of keycloak.realm.verifiableCredentials (see k3s/consumer.yaml).

The vc-operator requests the credential and keeps it renewed in a Secret, which is mounted into the Contract Management pod. It authenticates at Keycloak as a confidential client of its own, with the client credentials grant, so no user password is involved:

  1. A client in the realm for the Contract Management, with a service account and no other flow. The credential is issued to its service account user, so the roles it carries are the client roles of that user:

    keycloak:
  realm:
    clients:
      - clientId: contract-management
        enabled: true
        clientAuthenticatorType: client-secret
        secret: ${CM_CLIENT_SECRET}               # from a Secret, through keycloak.extraEnvVars
        publicClient: false
        serviceAccountsEnabled: true
        standardFlowEnabled: false
        directAccessGrantsEnabled: false
        protocol: openid-connect
        attributes:
          oid4vci.enabled: "true"
        optionalClientScopes: ["marketplace-credential"]
    users:
      - username: service-account-contract-management
        enabled: true
        serviceAccountClientId: contract-management
        clientRoles:
          <marketplace-DID>: [REPRESENTATIVE]
        verifiableCredentials:
          - credentialScopeName: marketplace-credential

  2. The credential request, with vcCredentials, which writes the credential into the vc-marketplace-credential Secret:

    vcCredentials:
  enabled: true
  issuers:
    - name: marketplace-issuer
      issuerURL: http://<release>-keycloak:8080/realms/<realm>
      issuerType: keycloak
      tokenURL: http://<release>-keycloak:8080/realms/<realm>/protocol/openid-connect/token
      auth:
        secretName: contract-management-client-auth
        clientId: contract-management
        clientSecret: <client-secret>             # or auth.existingSecret
      requests:
        - name: marketplace-credential
          credentialType: marketplace-credential  # the key under keycloak.realm.verifiableCredentials
          format: jwt_vc_json
          targetSecretName: vc-marketplace-credential
          targetSecretKey: credential
          renewBefore: 5m

vc-operator:
  enabled: true
  watchNamespaces: [<namespace>]

  3. The Secret in the Contract Management pod, in the folder oid4vp.credentialsFolder points to (step 1):

    contract-management:
  deployment:
    additionalVolumes:
      - name: credential-repo
        secret:
          secretName: vc-marketplace-credential
          items:
            - key: credential
              path: marketplace-credential.jwt
    additionalVolumeMounts:
      - name: credential-repo
        mountPath: /credential-repo

k3s/consumer-auth.yaml and k3s/consumer-tmf.yaml do the same for the local demo, together with a LegalPersonCredential.

docs.title: Authentication credential type
docs.text:
The MarketplaceCredential type is not mandatory — it is simply the type used throughout this documentation, the local demo and the shipped examples (see k3s/consumer.yaml Keycloak realm and k3s/provider.yaml policies). Any credential type can be used as long as the three sides agree on it:

  1. Keycloak (this realm) must issue the chosen type — adjust the verifiable_credential_type of its verifiableCredentials.<id> entry, the credentialType of the request under vcCredentials, and the file name the Secret is mounted as, which Contract Management reads.
  2. Central Marketplace VCVerifier + PAP use that same type to let its Contract Management present it to providers. No extra configuration is typically needed here.
  3. Each provider's VCVerifier + PAP must accept that type on the Contract Management endpoint (see step 3 and step 4 of Participating in a Central Marketplace — the type field in the service registered with vcverifier.registration.services and the allowContractManagement policy at the PAP).

If the type is changed, it must be changed consistently on all three sides or provider-side authentication will fail.

5. Authentication stack for the marketplace's own APIs

Providers and users accessing the catalog and ordering APIs authenticate via OID4VP against the marketplace's own VCVerifier + local Trusted Issuers List. The values mirror those of a Provider (see Provider role), but the services registered with vcverifier.registration.services must expose a LegalPersonCredential-based scope for the catalog/ordering endpoints (so any registered participant can log in to publish or buy offerings).

Note

The Central Marketplace does not deploy the ODRL-PAP + OPA data-service-protection stack. Its only protected surface is the TMForum API behind APISIX with OID4VP auth.

docs.title: k3s/ reference values
docs.text:
The local demo (mvn clean deploy -Plocal,central) deploys the Central Marketplace by reusing the consumer base chart together with two overlays that add the marketplace functionality. The same set of files can be used as a reference when preparing a production values file:

File Description k3s/consumer.yaml Base values for the organization hosting the Central Marketplace (Keycloak, DID, database, etc.) k3s/consumer-auth.yaml Authentication stack (VCVerifier, Trusted Issuers List, APISIX routes) required to protect the marketplace APIs k3s/consumer-tmf.yaml TMForum API, Scorpio backend and Contract Management configured in central-marketplace mode (enableCentralMarketplace: true, oid4vp.enabled: true)

Deploying the Central Marketplace with the same layout:

helm install central-marketplace oci://quay.io/fiware/helm-charts/data-space-connector --version <version> \
  -n central-marketplace \
  --create-namespace \
  -f k3s/consumer.yaml \
  -f k3s/consumer-auth.yaml \
  -f k3s/consumer-tmf.yaml

docs.title: Reference
docs.text:
• Architecture and end-to-end demo flow: CENTRAL_MARKETPLACE.md
  • Local demo deployment: mvn clean deploy -Plocal,central

docs.title: Helm chart
docs.text:
The Trust Anchor uses a dedicated Helm chart, separate from the participant chart, published next to it:

helm install trust-anchor oci://quay.io/fiware/helm-charts/trust-anchor --version <version> -n trust-anchor --create-namespace -f values.yaml
# or, from the Helm repository
helm repo add fiware-dsc https://fiware.github.io/data-space-connector
helm install trust-anchor fiware-dsc/trust-anchor --version <version> -n trust-anchor --create-namespace -f values.yaml

Start from the reference profile examples/trust-anchor.yaml, an example values file to adapt to your installation. Its README explains the prerequisites, the installation and how to register the participants.

docs.title: Dedicated infrastructure
docs.text: The Trust Anchor should be deployed on infrastructure managed independently from any participant: - Separate Kubernetes cluster, or at minimum a dedicated namespace with strict RBAC - Dedicated database instance (not shared with provider or consumer databases) - Independent operations team with its own access controls

docs.title: High availability
docs.text:
• Deploy the Trusted Issuers Registry with multiple replicas behind a load balancer
  • Ensure the TIR API remains available even during rolling updates

docs.title: Persistence and backups
docs.text:
• Enable persistence for the SQL database with durable storage
  • Configure automated backups with a recovery point objective (RPO) appropriate for your data space
  • Test restore procedures regularly
  • The Trust Anchor's data is critical: if it is lost, all participants lose their trust relationships

docs.title: TLS and network security
docs.text:
• Use valid TLS certificates from a real CA (not self-signed)
  • The TIR read API (/v4/issuers) should be publicly accessible (participants need to query it)
  • The TIL management API (/issuer) must be strictly restricted: only authorized operators should be able to register or remove issuers

docs.title: Integration with trust frameworks
docs.text: For production data spaces, consider integrating with established trust frameworks: - Gaia-X Digital Clearing Houses (GXDCH): for Gaia-X compliance. See Gaia-X Integration - EBSI: for European Blockchain Services Infrastructure compatibility - Custom trust frameworks defined by the data space governance body

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text: Key metrics to monitor: - TIR API availability and response times - Database connections and storage usage - Number of registered issuers (unexpected changes may indicate unauthorized access) - Certificate expiry dates - Audit logs of all management API operations (registrations, removals)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
A Provider is an organization that offers data services to other participants in the data space (e.g. APIs, data services web applications, etc). The provider hosts one or more services and protects them with a full decentralized identity and access management stack. Incoming requests must present valid Verifiable Credentials, which are verified against the data space's trust framework and evaluated against ODRL access policies.

These services can be: - APIs — RESTful APIs, NGSI-LD endpoints or any other HTTP-based service - Web applications — applications that integrate with Verifiable Credentials via OID4VC for user authentication and authorization

A provider may also needs the ability to issue its own Verifiable Credentials (for its employees or services), so it includes all the components of a Consumer plus additional authentication, authorization, and data service components.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
Before deploying, contact the Data Space Operator to initiate the onboarding process for your organization. The Operator will guide you through:

  • The documentation and requirements needed to join the data space
  • Registration of your organization's DID at the Trust Anchor
  • The credential types your organization is allowed to issue and their required configuration (claims, attribute mappings, etc.)
  • The Trust Anchor's TIR endpoint URL

This information is essential for configuring Keycloak, the DID, the VCVerifier, and the Verifiable Credentials correctly.

Check also that the cluster meets the Cluster Prerequisites: its databases, the network requirements and the resources the provider needs.

docs.title: Required components
docs.text:
Note

The data services that the provider wants to expose through the FIWARE Data Space Connector (APIs, web applications, etc.) are not included in this list. These are external to the connector and must be deployed and managed independently.

docs.title: Everything from the Consumer role
docs.text:
The provider needs the same base components as a consumer: - Keycloak — VC issuer for the provider's own users. For detailed configuration instructions, see the Keycloak Configuration guide. - DID Helper — publishes the provider's DID document - PostgreSQL — database for Keycloak and the IAM components: an existing one, or one the chart deploys (see Databases)

Note

If the data space uses the Decentralized Claims Protocol (DCP) (typically together with the Dataspace Protocol via FDSC-EDC), the DID Helper is replaced by the Identity Hub, which serves the DID document (and the provider's credentials) as required by DCP. See the Dataspace Protocol Integration Guide for details.

docs.title: Authentication: Verifiable Credential verification
docs.text: Component Description VCVerifier Verifies incoming Verifiable Credentials via OID4VP. Checks credential signatures, issuer trust (via the Trust Anchor), and credential type acceptance. Returns a JWT access token on success. Credentials configuration Which credential types are accepted for each protected service, and which Trusted Issuers Lists and Trusted Participants Lists to check. Served by the VCVerifier itself, on its configuration API (port 8090); the services are registered there from the values with vcverifier.registration.services. The standalone Credentials Config Service is no longer needed and is disabled by default. Trusted Issuers List (local) The provider's own list of trusted issuers, used in combination with the Trust Anchor's registry to determine which organizations can issue specific credential types.

docs.title: Authorization: Policy enforcement
docs.text: Component Description APISIX API Gateway that acts as the Policy Enforcement Point (PEP). Validates JWT tokens from VCVerifier and delegates authorization decisions to OPA. All external access to protected services goes through APISIX. OPA (Open Policy Agent) Policy Decision Point (PDP). Evaluates authorization policies (in Rego format, generated from ODRL) for each incoming request and returns allow/deny decisions. ODRL-PAP Policy Administration Point. Allows the provider to define access policies using ODRL (Open Digital Rights Language). Translates ODRL policies into Rego for OPA.

docs.title: Databases
docs.text:
Keycloak, the Trusted Issuers List, the VCVerifier, the ODRL-PAP and Scorpio store their data in PostgreSQL; the local marketplace also needs MongoDB (see Running a local marketplace). Use databases you already run, or let the chart deploy them:

  • A PostgreSQL deployed by the chart (decentralizedIam.vcAuthentication.managedPostgres, the default): a single cluster named postgres in the connector's namespace, with a database for each component, created by the Zalando Postgres Operator. The chart installs that operator by default too (decentralizedIam.vcAuthentication.postgres-operator.enabled); if one already runs in the cluster - for example installed by another connector or by the Trust Anchor - disable it in this release, since the operator's cluster-wide resources can only belong to one release.
  • An existing PostgreSQL: disable both, create a database and a user for each component, store the passwords in Secrets of the connector's namespace, and point each component to them:
decentralizedIam:
  vcAuthentication:
    managedPostgres:
      enabled: false
    postgres-operator:
      enabled: false
    trusted-issuers-list:
      database:
        host: <your_postgres_host>
        port: 5432
        name: <til_database>
        username: <til_user>
        existingSecret:
          enabled: true
          name: <til_secret>
          key: password
    vcverifier:
      deployment:
        database:
          host: <your_postgres_host>
          name: <verifier_database>
          existingSecret:
            name: <verifier_secret>               # holds both the user and the password
            usernameKey: username
            passwordKey: password
  odrlAuthorization:
    odrl-pap:
      database:
        url: jdbc:postgresql://<your_postgres_host>:5432/<pap_database>
        username: <pap_user>
        existingSecret:
          enabled: true
          name: <pap_secret>
          key: password
keycloak:
  database:
    host: <your_postgres_host>
    name: <keycloak_database>
    existingSecret: <keycloak_secret>             # holds both the user and the password
    secretKeys:
      usernameKey: username
      passwordKey: password
scorpio:
  db:
    dbhost: <your_postgres_host>
    user: <scorpio_user>
    existingSecret:
      enabled: true
      name: <scorpio_secret>
      key: password

Scorpio needs the PostGIS extension in its database; the examples in k3s/ create it, as a database named ngb, through the operator's preparedDatabases. The Identity Hub and the status list server, when enabled, take their database settings under identityhub.postgresql and statusListServer.postgresql.

The Trusted Issuers List and the Credentials Config Service apply their database migrations at startup - on the first start, and after an upgrade that brings new ones - holding a lock in the databasechangeloglock table of their database while they do. If the pod is killed in the middle of the migrations (out of memory, a failed node, a pod deleted during an upgrade), the lock stays set, and the next start logs Waiting for changelog lock.... and never completes. Release the lock in that database: the waiting pod then takes it and applies the remaining migrations. Do it only while no other pod of the service is applying them. With the chart's PostgreSQL, whose databases are tildb and ccsdb:

kubectl exec -n <namespace> postgres-0 -- psql -U postgres -d tildb \
  -c 'UPDATE databasechangeloglock SET locked = false, lockgranted = NULL, lockedby = NULL WHERE id = 1;'

docs.title: Optional components
docs.text:
All optional components listed below can be deployed using the fiware/data-space-connector Helm chart. Some of them - Scorpio, the TMForum API and Contract Management - are enabled by default; set them to false explicitly if you do not need them. The values example below lists the default of each one.

Note on Scorpio Context Broker

The FIWARE implementation of the TMForum APIs is based on NGSI-LD, which is why the fiware/data-space-connector Helm chart deploys a Scorpio Context Broker as its backend. In the provided examples, this same Scorpio instance is also used as the NGSI-LD endpoint that the provider exposes through the connector. However, in production, if you want to expose an NGSI-LD endpoint as a data service, you should deploy a separate Context Broker for that purpose and not reuse the Scorpio instance that backs the TMForum APIs.

docs.title: TMForum API
docs.text: The TMForum API implements standardized APIs for product catalog management, ordering, inventory, and more. These APIs are used both by the provider's own local marketplace and by the central marketplace if one exists in the data space. Enable this when: - You want to offer data products through a structured catalog - You need standardized product ordering workflows - You plan to use contract-based access control - You want to publish offerings to a central marketplace

docs.title: Contract Management
docs.text:
The Contract Management component automates access control based on product orders. When a consumer purchases a product offering via the TMForum API, Contract Management reacts to the order and registers the consumer's DID in the provider's local Trusted Issuers List, so the consumer's credentials are accepted at the provider when accessing the purchased service. The credential types granted to the consumer are taken from the ordered product. Additionally, if the ODRL-PAP is deployed, Contract Management also creates the ODRL access policies that encode the contract terms. Enable this when: - You use TMForum APIs for product ordering - Access should be granted/revoked automatically based on contracts - You need audit trails for data access agreements

Note

If the data space uses a central marketplace, the Contract Management component requires specific configuration to work with it. See the Central Marketplace documentation for details on how to configure Contract Management in that scenario.

Note

The policies and the credential configuration are read from the ordered ProductSpecification by default. A product can instead be composed of ServiceSpecifications that carry their own policies - an access policy protects an API, and in TMForum an API is a ServiceSpecification. See Authoring a composed ProductSpecification.

docs.title: Marketplace (BAE)
docs.text:
A provider can offer its products and services through a marketplace in two ways:

  • Local marketplace — Deploy a marketplace as part of the provider's own connector. The Business API Ecosystem provides a web portal for browsing and ordering product offerings directly from this provider. See Running a local marketplace.
  • Central marketplace — If the data space operates a shared central marketplace, the provider can publish its offerings there instead of (or in addition to) running its own. See the Central Marketplace documentation for details.

Enable the local marketplace when: - You want a user-facing web interface for your own data marketplace - Consumers should be able to browse and order offerings through a portal hosted by the provider

Note

The local Marketplace requires MongoDB in addition to the existing PostgreSQL, deployed by the chart through the MongoDB Community Operator. Running a local marketplace covers the whole setup: the operator, the values, the login with Verifiable Credentials and the security considerations.

Note

To create DSP-compatible products and offerings (i.e. offerings whose data is exchanged over the Dataspace Protocol — see FDSC-EDC (Dataspace Protocol)) through the local marketplace UI, the BAE Logic Proxy must be deployed with BAE_LP_DSP_ENABLED=true, set under marketplace.bizEcosystemLogicProxy.additionalEnvVars. This flag exposes the DSP-specific fields in the offering-creation forms; omit it for a marketplace that only brokers classic FIWARE offerings. See Using the BAE Marketplace in the DSP Integration documentation.

docs.title: Participating in a Central Marketplace
docs.text:
If the data space runs a shared Central Marketplace hosted by another actor (typically the Data Space Operator), the provider publishes its offerings there and does not deploy the marketplace itself. However, the provider's DSC needs specific configuration so the Central Marketplace can reach the local Contract Management and trigger the activation flow after each purchase.

Minimum versions

  • fiware/data-space-connector Helm chart ≥ 9.0.1
  • fiware/contract-management Helm chart ≥ 3.5.22
  • contract-management container image ≥ 3.3.8

The following configuration is required on the provider side. The example in k3s/provider.yaml already includes all of the pieces below and can be used as a reference.

1. Enable and configure Contract Management in central-marketplace mode

contract-management:
  enabled: true
  enableCentralMarketplace: true          # react to order notifications coming from an external marketplace
  enableOdrlPap: true                     # write ODRL policies to the local PAP on contract activation
  did: <your-organization-DID>
  til:
    credentialType: <YourCredentialType>  # e.g. OperatorCredential — registered in the local TIL on activation
  services:
    odrl:
      url: http://odrl-pap:8080
    # ... TMForum URLs, trusted-issuers-list, etc.
  notification:
    enabled: true
    host: contract-management
  deployment:
    image:
      tag: 3.3.8                          # minimum image required for central marketplace mode
  • enableCentralMarketplace activates the flow that reacts to order notifications coming from an external marketplace (instead of reacting to local orders only).
  • enableOdrlPap: true is required so that the ODRL policies attached to each purchased offering are installed in the provider's PAP when the contract is activated.
  • til.credentialType defines the credential type that Contract Management will register for each buyer in the local Trusted Issuers List when a purchase is completed.

2. Expose Contract Management externally through APISIX

The Central Marketplace sends order notifications to the provider's Contract Management over HTTPS, authenticating with its MarketplaceCredential. APISIX must expose the Contract Management on a dedicated host with the standard OIDC + OPA protection:

decentralizedIam:
  odrlAuthorization:
    apisix:
      ingress:
        hosts:
          - host: <your_contract_management_domain>    # e.g. provider-cm.example.org
            paths: ["/"]
      routes:
        # Well-known endpoint for Contract Management — proxied to the verifier
        - uri: /*/.well-known/openid-configuration
          host: <your_contract_management_domain>
          upstream:
            nodes:
              verifier:3000: 1
            type: roundrobin
          plugins:
            proxy-rewrite:
              uri: /services/contract-management/.well-known/openid-configuration
        # Catch-all route to Contract Management, protected by VCVerifier + OPA
        - uri: /*
          host: <your_contract_management_domain>
          upstream:
            nodes:
              contract-management:8080: 1
            type: roundrobin
          plugins:
            openid-connect:
              bearer_only: true
              use_jwks: true
              client_id: contract-management
              client_secret: unused
              ssl_verify: true            # see "Trusting a private CA" below if your certificates are not publicly trusted
              discovery: http://verifier:3000/services/contract-management/.well-known/openid-configuration
            opa:
              host: http://localhost:8181
              policy: policy/main
              with_body: true

3. Register the Contract Management as a service at the VCVerifier

The VCVerifier needs to know which credential types to accept on the Contract Management host. Register the service with a dedicated OIDC scope (external-marketplace) that accepts the MarketplaceCredential:

decentralizedIam:
  vcAuthentication:
    vcverifier:
      registration:
        enabled: true
        services:
          - id: contract-management
            defaultOidcScope: "external-marketplace"
            authorizationType: "DEEPLINK"
            oidcScopes:
              "external-marketplace":
                credentials:
                  - type: MarketplaceCredential
                    trustedParticipantsLists:
                      - <trust_anchor_tir_url>     # Trust Anchor's TIR endpoint
                    trustedIssuersLists:
                      - "*"                        # any issuer registered at the Trust Anchor
                    jwtInclusion:
                      enabled: true
                      fullInclusion: true

Add the entry to the same registration.services list as the provider's other services (such as the data-service of the values example): Helm replaces lists instead of merging them, so a list in a second values file drops the first one.

trustedIssuersLists: "*" is intentional here: the marketplace's credential is issued by the marketplace itself, and the trust decision is delegated entirely to the Trust Anchor's TIR.

4. Register the allowContractManagement policy at the PAP

Before receiving the first notification, the provider must install a policy at its PAP granting the Central Marketplace access to the Contract Management endpoint. See Prepare the provider (Step 1) in the Central Marketplace documentation for the exact policy and the curl command.

5. Register the provider as an Organization at the Central Marketplace

The Central Marketplace needs to know the provider's Contract Management endpoint and the OIDC client to authenticate with. This registration can be done through the TMForum API (partyCharacteristic.contractManagement) or through the Marketplace UI (Profile form). See Prepare the provider (Step 1) and Using the Marketplace UI in the Central Marketplace documentation for both variants.

docs.title: FDSC-EDC (Dataspace Protocol)
docs.text: Enable the Eclipse Dataspace Components connector for DSP compliance. See DSP Integration.

docs.title: Using the FIWARE DSC Helm chart and values
docs.text:
Start from the reference profile

examples/provider.yaml, and examples/provider-marketplace.yaml for the provider's own local marketplace (not the Central Marketplace), are complete values files for a provider, to adapt to your installation. Their README lists the prerequisites, the placeholders, the Secrets to create and the installation steps. The settings below explain each part.

The provider uses the fiware/data-space-connector chart with authentication and authorization components enabled.

Build a values.yaml for the provider by adapting examples/provider.yaml. The sections below show that file piece by piece and explain the key settings; replace every <placeholder>.

The ingresses use cert-manager through annotations and the ingress class you set, so adapt them to the controller your cluster runs (the local deployment uses Traefik). A ClusterIssuer is a prerequisite: use your own, or let the chart create one with certManagerResources (the examples README covers the prerequisites, Secrets and placeholders).

docs.title: Identity: did:web
docs.text:
did-helper serves the organization's did:web.
