Its key is the TLS certificate cert-manager issues for the ingress, and it must never rotate: a new key changes the DID, and every credential issued with the old one stops verifying (hence private-key-rotation-policy: Never; see Identity key lifecycle). did-helper also publishes that certificate at /.well-known/tls.crt, as the x5u of the key.

did:
  enabled: true
  config:
    server:
      # did-helper also publishes <hostUrl>/.well-known/tls.crt, the certificate of the key
      hostUrl: https://<did-domain>
      certPath: /certs/tls.crt
  volumes:
    - name: certs
      secret:
        # the DID's key: the certificate cert-manager issues for the ingress below
        secretName: did-tls
        items:
          - key: tls.crt
            path: tls.crt
  volumeMounts:
    - name: certs
      mountPath: /certs
  # with certPath did-helper writes nothing, so it runs on a read-only root filesystem
  securityContext:
    readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
    allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
    capabilities:
      drop: ["ALL"]
  ingress:
    enabled: true
    className: <ingress-class>
    annotations:
      cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: <cluster-issuer>
      cert-manager.io/private-key-algorithm: ECDSA
      # the Secret also holds the DID's key: a renewal must keep it, or the DID changes and every
      # credential issued with the old key stops verifying
      cert-manager.io/private-key-rotation-policy: Never
    hosts:
      - host: <did-domain>
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: ImplementationSpecific
    tls:
      - secretName: did-tls
        hosts:
          - <did-domain>

docs.title: Credential issuer: Keycloak
docs.text:
Keycloak issues the provider's own users their credentials and signs them with the DID's key: the prepare-keystore init container turns the DID Secret into the PKCS12 keystore the realm reads. The ingress publishes only /realms/<realm> and /resources; the admin console and the master realm stay inside the cluster. See Keycloak configuration.

keycloak:
  enabled: true
  keycloak:
    # the public URL, so that Keycloak does not derive it from each request
    hostname: https://<keycloak-domain>
    hostnameStrict: true
  # its own database user, created by the Postgres operator (see managedPostgres below)
  database:
    username: keycloak
    existingSecret: keycloak.postgres.credentials.postgresql.acid.zalan.do
  ingress:
    enabled: true
    className: <ingress-class>
    annotations:
      cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: <cluster-issuer>
      cert-manager.io/private-key-algorithm: ECDSA
    hosts:
      - host: <keycloak-domain>
        paths:
          # only what wallets need: the realm's endpoints and the static resources. The admin
          # console and the master realm stay inside the cluster (kubectl port-forward).
          - path: /realms/<realm>
            pathType: Prefix
          - path: /resources
            pathType: Prefix
    tls:
      - secretName: keycloak-tls
        hosts:
          - <keycloak-domain>
  # Keycloak signs the credentials with the DID's key: this init container turns the key and
  # certificate of the DID's Secret into the PKCS12 keystore the realm reads
  extraInitContainers:
    - name: prepare-keystore
      image: alpine/openssl:3.5.5
      command: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]
      args:
        - |
          # the CA of the certificate goes into the keystore too, when the Secret has it (a
          # private CA); a public one, such as Let's Encrypt, leaves ca.crt out or empty
          ca=""
          if [ -s /certs-did/ca.crt ]; then ca="-certfile /certs-did/ca.crt"; fi
          openssl pkcs12 -export \
            -in /certs-did/tls.crt \
            -inkey /certs-did/tls.key \
            $ca \
            -out /did-material/cert.pfx \
            -name "didPrivateKey" \
            -passout env:STORE_PASS
          chmod 644 /did-material/cert.pfx
      env:
        - name: STORE_PASS
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: keystore-password
              key: password
      volumeMounts:
        - name: did-material
          mountPath: /did-material
        - name: did-key
          mountPath: /certs-did
          readOnly: true
  extraVolumeMounts:
    # Keycloak only reads realm keystores from /opt/keycloak/data/<realm name>
    - name: did-material
      mountPath: /opt/keycloak/data/<realm>
    - name: realms
      mountPath: /opt/keycloak/data/import
  extraVolumes:
    - name: did-material
      emptyDir: {}
    # the realm the chart renders, in the ConfigMap <realm name>-realm
    - name: realms
      configMap:
        name: <realm>-realm
    - name: did-key
      secret:
        secretName: did-tls
  # replaces the chart's list: keep KC_HEAP_SIZE
  extraEnvVars:
    - name: KC_HEAP_SIZE
      value: "1024m"
    - name: STORE_PASS
      valueFrom:
        secretKeyRef:
          name: keystore-password
          key: password
  issuerDid: <did>
  signingKey:
    storePath: /opt/keycloak/data/<realm>/cert.pfx
    storePassword: "${STORE_PASS}"
    keyAlias: didPrivateKey
    keyPassword: "${STORE_PASS}"
    did: <did>
    keyAlgorithm: ES256
  realm:
    name: <realm>
    frontendUrl: https://<keycloak-domain>
    import: true
    # The provider's own staff get credentials too, for example to manage the provider's offers.
    # One credential type, UserCredential, with the roles the user holds at this provider.
    verifiableCredentials:
      user-credential:
        attributes:
          format: jwt_vc_json
          verifiable_credential_type: UserCredential
          credential_signing_alg: ES256
          credential_build_config.token_jws_type: JWT
        protocolMappers:
          - name: context-mapper
            protocol: oid4vc
            protocolMapper: oid4vc-context-mapper
            config:
              context: https://www.w3.org/2018/credentials/v1
          - name: email-mapper
            protocol: oid4vc
            protocolMapper: oid4vc-user-attribute-mapper
            config:
              claim.name: email
              userAttribute: email
          - name: roles-mapper
            protocol: oid4vc
            protocolMapper: oid4vc-target-role-mapper
            config:
              claim.name: roles
              clientId: <did>
          - name: subject-id-mapper
            protocol: oid4vc
            protocolMapper: oid4vc-subject-id-mapper
            config:
              userAttribute: email
              claim.name: id
    # Users are not part of the values: create them in the realm, or federate it.
    clientRoles: |
      "<did>": [
        {
          "name": "REPRESENTATIVE",
          "description": "Acts on behalf of the provider",
          "clientRole": true
        }
      ]
    # the client the roles above belong to, named after the DID. It only holds roles: no login
    # flow is enabled on it.
    clients: |
      {
        "clientId": "<did>",
        "description": "Roles of the users at this provider",
        "enabled": true,
        "protocol": "openid-connect",
        "publicClient": false,
        "standardFlowEnabled": false,
        "implicitFlowEnabled": false,
        "directAccessGrantsEnabled": false,
        "serviceAccountsEnabled": false
      }

docs.title: Authentication and authorization
docs.text:
The verifier checks each request's credentials against the Trust Anchor's registry (tirAddress) and the provider's local trusted issuers list, and issues access tokens signed with a persistent RSA key. APISIX is the gateway in standalone mode with its Admin API disabled, OPA decides on the ODRL policies the PAP holds, and each component connects to its own PostgreSQL user. If the certificates in the chain are not publicly trusted, see Trusting a private CA for ssl_verify.

decentralizedIam:
  enabled: true
  vcAuthentication:
    # the Postgres operator is installed once per cluster, not by each release
    postgres-operator:
      enabled: false
    # One PostgreSQL cluster for the provider's components, each with its own user. The operator
    # creates the users and a Secret with each password.
    managedPostgres:
      enabled: true
      config:
        volume:
          size: 10Gi
          # storageClass: <storage-class>
        # Scorpio's database, with PostGIS. Scorpio connects as its owner, ngb_owner_user.
        preparedDatabases:
          ngb:
            defaultUsers: true
            schemas:
              public: {}
            extensions:
              postgis: public

    # The provider's trusted issuers list: which participants may issue which credentials to
    # the users of this provider's services. Internal only: entries are added by the
    # `registration` below or through its API inside the cluster.
    trusted-issuers-list:
      database:
        username: til
        existingSecret:
          enabled: true
          name: til.postgres.credentials.postgresql.acid.zalan.do
          key: password

    vcverifier:
      ingress:
        enabled: true
        className: <ingress-class>
        annotations:
          cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: <cluster-issuer>
          cert-manager.io/private-key-algorithm: ECDSA
        hosts:
          - host: <verifier-domain>
            paths:
              - /
        tls:
          - secretName: verifier-tls
            hosts:
              - <verifier-domain>
      deployment:
        database:
          existingSecret:
            name: ccs.postgres.credentials.postgresql.acid.zalan.do
        server:
          host: https://<verifier-domain>
        verifier:
          did: <did>
          # the trust anchor's registry of the data space's participants
          tirAddress: <tir-url>
          supportedModes: ["byValue", "byReference"]
          # request objects are signed with the key of the verifier's own TLS certificate
          clientIdentification:
            id: x509_san_dns:<verifier-domain>
            keyPath: /client-key/tls.key
            certificatePath: /client-key/tls.crt
            requestKeyAlgorithm: ES256
          # the access tokens are signed with a persistent RSA key (verifier-token-key, at the end
          # of this file), not with one generated on every start
          generateKey: false
          keyAlgorithm: RS256
          keyPath: /token-key/tls.key
        serverCertificates:
          signingKey:
            secretName: verifier-token-key
            key: tls.key
        additionalVolumes:
          - name: client-key
            secret:
              secretName: verifier-tls
        additionalVolumeMounts:
          - name: client-key
            mountPath: /client-key
            readOnly: true
      # The services the verifier issues tokens for, and the credentials each one accepts.
      # Registered on install and upgrade; a service that already exists is left as it is.
      registration:
        enabled: true
        services:
          - id: data-service
            defaultOidcScope: default
            authorizationType: DEEPLINK
            oidcScopes:
              default:
                credentials:
                  - type: UserCredential
                    trustedParticipantsLists:
                      - <tir-url>
                    trustedIssuersLists:
                      - http://trusted-issuers-list:8080
          - id: tmf-api
            defaultOidcScope: default
            authorizationType: DEEPLINK
            oidcScopes:
              default:
                credentials:
                  - type: UserCredential
                    trustedParticipantsLists:
                      - <tir-url>
                    trustedIssuersLists:
                      - http://trusted-issuers-list:8080

  odrlAuthorization:
    odrl-pap:
      database:
        username: pap
        existingSecret:
          enabled: true
          name: pap.postgres.credentials.postgresql.acid.zalan.do
          key: password
      additionalEnvVars:
        - name: GENERAL_ORGANIZATION_DID
          value: <did>
    apisix:
      apisix:
        # routes come from the values (standalone mode): the Admin API is not needed
        admin:
          enabled: false
      ingress:
        enabled: true
        className: <ingress-class>
        annotations:
          cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: <cluster-issuer>
          cert-manager.io/private-key-algorithm: ECDSA
        hosts:
          - host: <data-service-domain>
            paths: ["/"]
          - host: <tmf-domain>
            paths: ["/"]
        tls:
          - secretName: apisix-tls
            hosts:
              - <data-service-domain>
              - <tmf-domain>
      routes:
        # the data service: OpenID discovery, served by the verifier ...
        - uri: /.well-known/openid-configuration
          host: <data-service-domain>
          upstream:
            nodes:
              verifier:3000: 1
            type: roundrobin
          plugins:
            proxy-rewrite:
              uri: /services/data-service/.well-known/openid-configuration
        # ... and every other request, with a token of the verifier and allowed by the policies
        - uri: /*
          host: <data-service-domain>
          upstream:
            nodes:
              <data-service-upstream>: 1
            type: roundrobin
          plugins:
            openid-connect:
              bearer_only: true
              use_jwks: true
              client_id: data-service
              client_secret: unused
              ssl_verify: true
              discovery: https://<verifier-domain>/services/data-service/.well-known/openid-configuration
            opa:
              host: http://localhost:8181
              policy: policy/main
              with_body: true
        # the TM Forum API (offers, orders), protected the same way
        - uri: /.well-known/openid-configuration
          host: <tmf-domain>
          upstream:
            nodes:
              verifier:3000: 1
            type: roundrobin
          plugins:
            proxy-rewrite:
              uri: /services/tmf-api/.well-known/openid-configuration
        - uri: /*
          host: <tmf-domain>
          upstream:
            nodes:
              tm-forum-api-svc:8080: 1
            type: roundrobin
          plugins:
            openid-connect:
              bearer_only: true
              use_jwks: true
              client_id: tmf-api
              client_secret: unused
              ssl_verify: true
              discovery: https://<verifier-domain>/services/tmf-api/.well-known/openid-configuration
            opa:
              host: http://localhost:8181
              policy: policy/main
              with_body: true

# The participants whose credentials this provider accepts, registered in its trusted issuers
# list on install and upgrade: here, a consumer issuing UserCredentials to its users.
registration:
  enabled: true
  til: http://trusted-issuers-list:8080
  issuer:
    - did: <consumer-did>
      credentialTypes:
        - UserCredential

docs.title: Offers and contracts
docs.text:
Scorpio stores the TM Forum data and the TM Forum API serves it; both stay internal, reachable only through APISIX. contract-management turns completed orders into ODRL policies at the PAP.

# Scorpio stores the TM Forum data. Keep it internal: it is not the public data service.
scorpio:
  db:
    user: ngb_owner_user
    existingSecret:
      enabled: true
      name: ngb-owner-user.postgres.credentials.postgresql.acid.zalan.do
      key: password

# All the TM Forum APIs in one deployment, served as tm-forum-api-svc. Internal: published only
# through APISIX (above).
tm-forum-api:
  allInOne:
    enabled: true
  apiProxy:
    enabled: false

contract-management:
  did: <did>
  # turns completed orders into ODRL policies at the PAP
  enableOdrlPap: true
  services:
    product-order:
      url: http://tm-forum-api-svc:8080
    party:
      url: http://tm-forum-api-svc:8080
    product-catalog:
      url: http://tm-forum-api-svc:8080
    service-catalog:
      url: http://tm-forum-api-svc:8080
    tmforum-agreement-api:
      url: http://tm-forum-api-svc:8080
    quote:
      url: http://tm-forum-api-svc:8080

docs.title: Signing key
docs.text:
The verifier's token-signing key is a persistent RSA key kept in a Secret, so access tokens stay valid across restarts and replicas.

extraManifests:
  # the verifier's token signing key: RSA, kept in a Secret so that tokens stay valid across
  # restarts and replicas
  - apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
    kind: Certificate
    metadata:
      name: verifier-token-key
      namespace: "{{ .Release.Namespace }}"
    spec:
      secretName: verifier-token-key
      commonName: <verifier-domain>
      dnsNames:
        - <verifier-domain>
      issuerRef:
        name: <cluster-issuer>
        kind: ClusterIssuer
      privateKey:
        algorithm: RSA
        size: 2048

docs.title: Optional components
docs.text: scorpio, tm-forum-api and contract-management are part of the profile because a provider that offers TM Forum products needs them; a provider that only protects a plain data service can set them to false. Other components are optional and off by default: a local marketplace (examples/provider-marketplace.yaml), the Dataspace Protocol connector (DSP Integration), and Vault for production identity material (Production setup for Vault).

docs.title: Install the chart
docs.text:
Install the chart with your values, pinning its version (see the release notes for what changes between versions):

helm install provider oci://quay.io/fiware/helm-charts/data-space-connector \
  --version <version> \
  -n provider \
  --create-namespace \
  -f provider-values.yaml

The chart is also available from the Helm repository https://fiware.github.io/data-space-connector:

helm repo add fiware-dsc https://fiware.github.io/data-space-connector
helm install provider fiware-dsc/data-space-connector --version <version> -n provider --create-namespace -f provider-values.yaml

See the reference profile examples/provider.yaml for a complete example.

docs.title: Other deployment options
docs.text:
A base example for a provider deployment can be found at k3s/provider.yaml.

Note

These values are intended for local development and testing environments. For a real production deployment, they must be customized to meet your infrastructure, security, and availability requirements. See Production considerations below.

For other deployment scenarios, the base provider.yaml can be extended with additional overlay values files (which take precedence over the base). The following overlays are available:

Overlay File Description eIDAS / ELSI k3s/provider-eidas.yaml Configuration for deployments compliant with the ELSI trust framework, including eIDAS 2.0 trust list validation via VCVerifier's built-in PKIX chain verification against the EU Trusted Lists Gaia-X k3s/provider-gaia-x.yaml Configuration for Gaia-X compliant deployments DSP k3s/dsp-provider.yaml Enables the Dataspace Protocol (DSP) connector on the provider side

For example, to deploy a provider with ELSI compliance:

helm install provider oci://quay.io/fiware/helm-charts/data-space-connector --version <version> \
  -n provider \
  -f k3s/provider.yaml \
  -f k3s/provider-eidas.yaml

docs.title: TLS certificates
docs.text:
• All publicly reachable endpoints must use HTTPS with valid TLS certificates issued by a trusted CA
  • You can enable cert-manager directly in the FIWARE DSC Helm chart to automate certificate issuance and renewal

docs.title: DID and key management
docs.text:
• Use a registered domain name that your organization controls for the did:web identifier
  • Ensure the DID document is served over HTTPS with a valid certificate
  • Protect the private key associated with your DID: it is the foundation of your organization's identity in the data space. If compromised, an attacker could issue credentials on your behalf

docs.title: Identity key lifecycle
docs.text:
The DID's private key is what did-helper publishes and what Keycloak signs credentials with. If it changes, the DID document changes with it, every credential signed with the previous key stops verifying, and the participants that resolved the DID see a different key without notice.

Since cert-manager 1.18, a certificate's privateKey.rotationPolicy defaults to Always: every renewal - every 60 days with Let's Encrypt - generates a new key. Whatever certificate holds the DID's key must therefore set Never. There are two ways to do it:

  • On the DID's Ingress, as the example above does: the cert-manager.io/private-key-rotation-policy: "Never" annotation makes cert-manager keep the key of the certificate it issues for that Ingress, and the same Secret serves TLS and holds the identity key. It is the smallest change, but ties the identity to that Ingress: changing its controller, host or issuer touches the identity key too.
  • A dedicated Certificate for the identity, separate from any Ingress, which only cert-manager renews and which keeps its key. Mount its Secret in did-helper and in the Keycloak keystore init container (Keycloak guide) instead of the Ingress' one; the Ingresses keep their own certificates, so a TLS rotation or compromise does not reach the identity:
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: Certificate
metadata:
  name: identity-key
  namespace: <your_namespace>
spec:
  secretName: <your_identity_key_secret>
  commonName: <your_did_domain>
  dnsNames:
    - <your_did_domain>
  issuerRef:
    name: <your_cluster_issuer>
    kind: ClusterIssuer
  privateKey:
    algorithm: ECDSA
    size: 256
    rotationPolicy: Never      # renewals keep the key, and with it the DID

Either way, every component that holds a copy of the key has to follow it: restarting did-helper and Keycloak on a changed Secret keeps them consistent, but credentials signed with a previous key still stop verifying, and a component that stored the key elsewhere - such as the identity hub, in Vault - keeps the old one. Hence Never.

Use separate keys for everything else that signs, such as the verifier's request objects (clientIdentification) and tokens (see VCVerifier): sharing the identity key spreads it across components that do not need it. The local marketplace needs no key of its own when it logs users in through the verifier's OpenID Connect discovery, as Running a local marketplace describes; its SIOP mode, instead, has to sign with the identity key itself, since the verifier checks those signatures against the DID.

Keep a backup of the identity key outside the cluster: losing it means a new DID. Rotating it on purpose works the same way as losing it - did-helper publishes a single key - so plan it as a re-issuance of the credentials signed with the old one, as described for the identity hub in Vault.

docs.title: Do not expose internal APIs
docs.text: The following ingresses are useful for development but must not be publicly accessible in production: - Scorpio Broker direct ingress — all access must go through APISIX - ODRL-PAP ingress — policy management should be restricted to authorized operators - Trusted Issuers List management API — restrict to internal access - VCVerifier configuration API (vcverifier.configIngress, port 8090) — it defines which credentials each service accepts; keep it internal, and only publish it, restricted, if services have to be managed from outside the cluster

docs.title: APISIX configuration
docs.text:
• Publish the gateway through its Ingress (decentralizedIam.odrlAuthorization.apisix.ingress), which carries the host and TLS. Its Service is a ClusterIP one by default; making it a NodePort or LoadBalancer (apisix.service.type) opens the gateway outside of the Ingress as well
  • APISIX's etcd is only deployed when apisix.etcd.enabled is set, and only needed in a mode that reads the configuration from it, such as traditional with config_provider: etcd (the mode the routes registered through the Admin API need). The default standalone mode reads the routes from a ConfigMap. A mode that needs etcd without one fails to render
  • Change the APISIX admin credentials from defaults
  • Configure proper error responses (do not leak internal service details)
  • Keep ssl_verify: true in the openid-connect plugin. Even when discovery points to the verifier inside the cluster, the discovery document announces the verifier's public jwks_uri, so APISIX fetches the keys that validate every token over HTTPS. Without verification, whoever can intercept that call can make APISIX accept forged tokens.

docs.title: Trusting a private CA
docs.text:
If the verifier's certificate is issued by a private CA, give APISIX that CA instead of disabling the verification. Put the CA certificate (PEM) in a Secret, for example private-ca with the key ca.crt, and point the apisix chart to it:

decentralizedIam:
  odrlAuthorization:
    apisix:
      apisix:
        ssl:
          enabled: true              # the chart only mounts the CA together with its HTTPS listener
          existingCASecret: private-ca
          certCAFilename: ca.crt

The apisix chart only mounts the CA, and sets it as APISIX's ssl_trusted_certificate, when apisix.ssl.enabled is set, which also opens its HTTPS listener (port 9443); that listener needs no further configuration when TLS is terminated at the Ingress.

docs.title: VCVerifier
docs.text:
• Configure the tirAddress to point to the production Trust Anchor's TIR endpoint
  • Ensure the VCVerifier can reach the Trust Anchor over HTTPS with valid certificates
  • If using a proxy, configure HTTPS_PROXY/NO_PROXY appropriately
  • The VCVerifier's signing key (used for JWT issuance) must be protected

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text: The verifier serves its Prometheus metrics, /metrics, on port 9090 of the verifier Service (metrics), apart from port 3000, which its Ingress publishes, so the metrics are not reachable from outside the cluster. Scrape them from inside the cluster, at http://verifier.<your_namespace>.svc.cluster.local:9090/metrics. The port is set with deployment.server.metricsPort; setting it to the main port (3000) serves the metrics there again, and publishes them with the Ingress.

docs.title: Request object modes
docs.text:
deployment.verifier.supportedModes defaults to urlEncoded. With byValue or byReference the verifier signs the request objects it sends to wallets, so it also needs clientIdentification; without its keyPath the verifier does not start (Failed to initialize verifier):

decentralizedIam:
  vcAuthentication:
    vcverifier:
      deployment:
        verifier:
          supportedModes: ["byValue", "byReference"]
          clientIdentification:
            id: x509_san_dns:<your_verifier_domain>   # how the verifier identifies itself to wallets
            keyPath: /signing-key/tls.key            # key that signs the request objects
            certificatePath: /signing-key/tls.crt    # certificate embedded in their header
            requestKeyAlgorithm: ES256               # algorithm of that key
        additionalVolumes:
          - name: signing-key
            secret:
              secretName: <your_verifier_domain>-tls # e.g. a cert-manager certificate for the verifier's domain
        additionalVolumeMounts:
          - name: signing-key
            mountPath: /signing-key

The verifier reads the algorithm from requestKeyAlgorithm; the keyAlgorithm listed under clientIdentification in the vcverifier chart's values has no effect.

docs.title: Token signing algorithm
docs.text:
The access tokens the verifier issues are validated by APISIX's openid-connect plugin, whose library (lua-resty-openidc) only accepts tokens signed with RS* or HS* algorithms, in every APISIX version up to 3.19 at least. With an ES256 token it does not look up any key - neither in the JWKS nor in an x5c chain - and rejects every request with 401 and jwt signature verification failed: No trusted certs loaded. Keep deployment.verifier.keyAlgorithm at its default RS256 for every verifier whose tokens APISIX validates. This only concerns the verifier's tokens; Keycloak can keep signing credentials with ES256.

By default (generateKey: true) the verifier generates that key at startup and only keeps it in memory, so the tokens issued before a restart stop validating and several replicas do not share a key. In production, provide an RSA key instead, with generateKey: false and keyPath.

docs.title: Policy management
docs.text:
• Define ODRL policies following the principle of least privilege
  • Consider versioning your policies (store them in version control and apply via CI/CD)

docs.title: Central Marketplace integration
docs.text:
If the provider participates in a Central Marketplace:

  • The Contract Management host exposed through APISIX must be reachable from the Central Marketplace over HTTPS with a valid certificate. The contractManagement.address registered in the provider's Organization at the marketplace must match this host exactly: no trailing paths, and the scheme/port used when registering must remain valid from the marketplace's network.
  • Coordinate version upgrades with the Central Marketplace operator: changes in the contract-management notification contract require both sides to be aligned. Keep the minimum versions noted in Participating in a Central Marketplace as a floor.
  • Keep the local Trusted Issuers List aligned with the Central Marketplace's MarketplaceCredential issuer. If the marketplace rotates its DID, the provider will stop accepting notifications until the TIL and the Trust Anchor's TIR are updated.

docs.title: Upgrade strategy
docs.text:
• Review the FIWARE Data Space Connector release notes before each upgrade for breaking changes
  • Keep the connector version aligned across all participants in the data space when possible to avoid protocol incompatibilities

docs.title: Authoring a composed ProductSpecification
docs.text:
An access policy protects an API, and in TMForum an API is a ServiceSpecification. A provider selling one product built from three services can therefore author three policies where they belong, instead of merging them into one policy on the ProductSpecification.

contract-management reads the configuration of the composed ServiceSpecifications when it activates an order. This page is the provider's view of that: how to switch it on, how to author it, and which rules decide what a customer ends up being allowed to do.

docs.title: Switching it on
docs.text:
contract-management:
  # read the configuration of the composed ServiceSpecifications as well
  enableSpecificationComposition: true
  # how many specification levels below the ordered product are resolved
  specificationCompositionMaxDepth: 2
Component Minimum version contract-management chart 3.5.36 (app 3.3.12) trusted-issuers-list app 0.9.1

Both ship with the connector chart; no image override is needed. See the 10.8.0 release note.

Leaving the flag off keeps the previous behaviour exactly: only the ordered ProductSpecification is read.

docs.title: Which characteristic belongs where
docs.text:
The split is deliberate: the enforcement plane moves down to the service, the DSP description plane stays at the product.

Characteristic Level Read by authorizationPolicy ServiceSpecification (product level still works for product-wide rules) contract-management → ODRL-PAP purpose ServiceSpecification consent-facade credentialsConfiguration ProductSpecification, additionally allowed per service contract-management → trusted-issuers-list endpointUrl, endpointDescription, transferType, transferPath ProductSpecification fdsc-edc (DSP catalog) upstreamAddress, serviceConfiguration, targetSpecification ProductSpecification fdsc-transfer-extension

The last two rows exist for the DSP integration, and DSP has no notion of a composed product: one ProductSpecification is one dataset with one set of distributions. Authoring them on a ServiceSpecification would put them where nothing reads them.

docs.title: The container names differ
docs.text:
The same concept is spelled differently per API. This is the most common authoring mistake:

Entity Characteristic list Value list ProductSpecification productSpecCharacteristic productSpecCharacteristicValue ServiceSpecification specCharacteristic characteristicValueSpecification

id, name and valueType are the same on both, and valueType is what the connector discriminates on. A characteristic without a valueType is skipped.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
Continuing the "M&P K8S" example of the local deployment: the product is composed of one service that carries the cluster-creation policy.

1 — the service specification, with the policy

export SERVICE_SPEC_ID=$(curl -k -x localhost:8888 -X 'POST' https://tm-forum-api.127.0.0.1.nip.io/tmf-api/serviceCatalogManagement/v4/serviceSpecification \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json;charset=utf-8' \
  -d "{
    \"name\": \"M&P K8S Cluster API\",
    \"version\": \"1.0.0\",
    \"lifecycleStatus\": \"ACTIVE\",
    \"specCharacteristic\": [
      {
        \"id\": \"policyConfig\",
        \"name\": \"Policy for creation of K8S clusters.\",
        \"valueType\": \"authorizationPolicy\",
        \"characteristicValueSpecification\": [
          {
            \"isDefault\": true,
            \"value\": {
              \"@context\": { \"odrl\": \"http://www.w3.org/ns/odrl/2/\" },
              \"@id\": \"https://mp-operation.org/policy/common/k8s-small\",
              \"odrl:uid\": \"https://mp-operation.org/policy/common/k8s-small\",
              \"@type\": \"odrl:Policy\",
              \"odrl:permission\": {
                \"odrl:assigner\": \"https://www.mp-operation.org/\",
                \"odrl:target\": {
                  \"@type\": \"odrl:AssetCollection\",
                  \"odrl:source\": \"urn:asset\",
                  \"odrl:refinement\": [
                    {
                      \"@type\": \"odrl:Constraint\",
                      \"odrl:leftOperand\": \"ngsi-ld:entityType\",
                      \"odrl:operator\": \"odrl:eq\",
                      \"odrl:rightOperand\": \"K8SCluster\"
                    }
                  ]
                },
                \"odrl:action\": \"odrl:use\"
              }
            }
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }" | jq -r '.id')

2 — the product specification, referencing it

The credential configuration stays at the product level: it describes what the customer's issuer may assert, which is a commercial fact about the product rather than about one of its APIs.

export PRODUCT_SPEC_ID=$(curl -k -x localhost:8888 -X 'POST' https://tm-forum-api.127.0.0.1.nip.io/tmf-api/productCatalogManagement/v4/productSpecification \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json;charset=utf-8' \
  -d "{
    \"brand\": \"M&P Operations\",
    \"version\": \"1.0.0\",
    \"lifecycleStatus\": \"ACTIVE\",
    \"name\": \"M&P K8S Small\",
    \"serviceSpecification\": [
      { \"id\": \"${SERVICE_SPEC_ID}\" }
    ],
    \"productSpecCharacteristic\": [
      {
        \"id\": \"credentialsConfig\",
        \"name\": \"Credentials Config\",
        \"valueType\": \"credentialsConfiguration\",
        \"productSpecCharacteristicValue\": [
          {
            \"isDefault\": true,
            \"value\": {
              \"credentialsType\": \"OperatorCredential\",
              \"claims\": [
                {
                  \"name\": \"roles\",
                  \"path\": \"$.roles[?(@.target==\\\"${PROVIDER_DID}\\\")].names[*]\",
                  \"allowedValues\": [ \"OPERATOR\" ]
                }
              ]
            }
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }" | jq -r '.id')

The referenced service specification has to exist first: the TMForum API validates the reference and rejects the product specification otherwise.

3 — the offering is unchanged: it references the ProductSpecification as before.

Ordering that offering now installs the service's policy at the ODRL-PAP and grants the product's credential configuration at the trusted-issuers-list.

docs.title: The rules that decide what a customer may do
docs.text:
Union, never override. The effective configuration of a product is the union over the product and its services. No level narrows another.

Credential configurations widen. The trusted-issuers-list evaluates several configurations of one credential type as an OR, so a permissive entry relaxes a restrictive one. If a service is part of a "small" and a "full" product, the small product's customer is not restricted by the small product's entry alone; author the restriction where it is not shared, or split the service.

Policies are keyed by odrl:uid. Identical policies from several parts are installed once. Two different policies claiming the same odrl:uid fail the activation, because the ODRL-PAP keys an installed policy by that uid plus the order id and could only ever keep one of them. Give every policy its own uid.

One provider per composition. A ServiceSpecification whose relatedParty names a different provider than the product fails the activation. A part that names no provider inherits the product's one, which is what the marketplace produces. Composing across providers is not supported.

The order is a snapshot. The configuration is resolved when the order completes, and not re-resolved when a specification changes afterwards. Editing a shared service specification does not retroactively change what existing orders granted.

Revocation is per order. Credentials are granted at the trusted-issuers-list under the id of the order that granted them, so cancelling one order leaves what another order granted in place, which is what makes sharing a service specification safe.

docs.title: When something does not activate
docs.text:
contract-management says what it did or refused to do. The lines worth grepping for:

Log line Meaning The composition of specification … is deeper than the configured limit of N levels references deeper than the limit were not applied. Raise specificationCompositionMaxDepth or flatten the composition The composition of specification … contains two different policies claiming the uid … two parts use one odrl:uid for different policies; nothing was installed The composition of specification … declares more than one provider a part names a different provider party The … specification … referenced by specification … could not be resolved a dangling reference — the catalog is broken, and the activation failed rather than granting a partial configuration The offering … does not reference a product specification a bundled offering; it configures nothing by itself The trusted-issuers-list rejected the credentials granted by order … with status 404 the deployed trusted-issuers-list is older than 0.9.1

A truncation is the one case that leaves an order partially activated, which is why it is logged as a warning naming the specification and the references it skipped.

docs.title: Running a local marketplace
docs.text:
A provider can run its own marketplace, the Business API Ecosystem (BAE), as part of its connector: a web portal where its offerings are published, browsed and ordered. This guide sets it up with the data-space-connector chart, for a provider that already follows the provider guide.

If the data space runs a shared marketplace instead, see Participating in a Central Marketplace. For the local demo with a mobile wallet, see Marketplace integration.

  • What gets deployed
  • Prerequisites
  • MongoDB
  • Values
  • TMForum API and contract management
  • The chart's MongoDB
  • The marketplace
  • Login with Verifiable Credentials
  • Trusting a private CA
  • Common mistakes
  • Security
  • Installing and checking it

docs.title: What gets deployed
docs.text:
Component Role BAE logic proxy (marketplace.bizEcosystemLogicProxy) The portal and the API the portal uses BAE charging backend (marketplace.bizEcosystemChargingBackend) Orders, billing and the assets attached to offerings TMForum API (tm-forum-api) Where offerings, orders and parties are stored; the BAE is a front end for it MongoDB The BAE's own data: an existing MongoDB, or one the chart deploys (managedMongo) Contract management (contract-management) Reacts to completed orders: grants the buyer access in the trusted issuers list and installs the policies of the ordered product VCVerifier Users log in to the portal by presenting a Verifiable Credential

The data service itself, Keycloak, the DID and the VCVerifier are the ones of the provider deployment.

docs.title: MongoDB
docs.text:
The marketplace stores its data in MongoDB. Use the one you already have, or let the chart deploy one:

Option When What it needs An existing MongoDB You already run one, or several connectors share one managedMongo.enabled: false, and the marketplace's databases, users and passwords created in it. See Using an existing MongoDB A MongoDB deployed by the chart (managedMongo) You have none A MongoDB operator in the cluster. The chart creates a MongoDBCommunity named mongodb in the connector's namespace, with the marketplace's users

docs.title: The operator, for a MongoDB deployed by the chart
docs.text:
managedMongo needs an operator that handles MongoDBCommunity resources: the MongoDB Community Operator, whose chart the connector pins (community-operator in Chart.yaml, 0.13.0 at the time of writing), or its successor MongoDB Controllers for Kubernetes, which manages the same resource. The operator is cluster-wide: install it once, outside the connector, and leave mongo-operator.enabled: false (the default) in the connector's values. The Cluster Prerequisites explain why each operator can be installed only once per cluster.

Install it with watchNamespace: "*", which lets it manage databases outside its own namespace:

helm repo add mongodb https://mongodb.github.io/helm-charts
helm install mongo-operator mongodb/community-operator --version 0.13.0 \
  -n mongo-operator --create-namespace \
  --set operator.watchNamespace="*"

The MongoDB pods run as a service account of the chart's own, <release>-mongodb, with its Role and RoleBinding (managedMongo.serviceAccount), so the operator's database.namespace does not matter: it only says where the operator's chart creates its own mongodb-database. To run them as a service account you manage yourself, set managedMongo.serviceAccount.create: false and its name; without a name, they run as the operator's mongodb-database, which then has to exist in the connector's namespace.

docs.title: Database passwords
docs.text:
The chart's MongoDB has three users: admin, and one for each marketplace component (charging, belp). Their passwords come from three Secrets, each with a password key:

Secret User mongodb-admin-password admin mongodb-charging-password charging (charging backend) mongodb-belp-password belp (logic proxy)

With marketplace.generatePasswords: true (the default), the chart generates them on the first install, with random values, and keeps them on upgrade and uninstall. That is convenient for a test environment. In production, create them yourself beforehand - from your secret store, External Secrets or Sealed Secrets - and set generatePasswords: false.

docs.title: Using an existing MongoDB
docs.text:
Create a database and a user with readWrite on it for each marketplace component, store each password in a Secret of the connector's namespace, and point the components to them:

managedMongo:
  enabled: false
marketplace:
  generatePasswords: false
  bizEcosystemChargingBackend:
    existingSecret: <charging_password_secret>   # the password under the key below
    db:
      host: <your_mongodb_host>
      database: <charging_database>
      user: <charging_user>
      secretKey: password
  bizEcosystemLogicProxy:
    existingSecret: <logic_proxy_password_secret>
    db:
      host: <your_mongodb_host>
      database: <logic_proxy_database>
      user: <logic_proxy_user>
      secretKey: password

docs.title: Values
docs.text: The values below go into the provider's values file, next to those of the provider guide. Replace the placeholders; <your_did> is the provider's DID.

docs.title: TMForum API and contract management
docs.text:
Both are enabled by default; the marketplace needs them configured as follows:

tm-forum-api:
  enabled: true
  allInOne:
    enabled: true          # all TMForum APIs in one deployment, served as tm-forum-api-svc
  apiProxy:
    enabled: false         # not needed with allInOne
  ingress:
    enabled: false         # reach it through APISIX only, see Security

contract-management:
  enabled: true
  did: <your_did>
  enableOdrlPap: true
  enableTrustedIssuersList: true
  organization:
    provider:
      role: seller         # the BAE records the provider of an offering with the role "seller"
  services:
    trusted-issuers-list:
      url: http://trusted-issuers-list:8080
    product-order:
      url: http://tm-forum-api-svc:8080
    party:
      url: http://tm-forum-api-svc:8080
    product-catalog:
      url: http://tm-forum-api-svc:8080
    service-catalog:
      url: http://tm-forum-api-svc:8080
    tmforum-agreement-api:
      url: http://tm-forum-api-svc:8080
    quote:
      url: http://tm-forum-api-svc:8080
    odrl:
      url: http://odrl-pap:8080

organization.provider.role is the relatedParty role by which contract management finds the provider of an ordered product. The chart default is provider, while the BAE records the provider as seller: without the setting, contract management does not find the provider of the orders placed in the BAE and activates nothing.

docs.title: The chart's MongoDB
docs.text:
When the chart deploys MongoDB:

managedMongo:
  enabled: true
  spec:
    version: "8.0.12"      # the chart defaults to 6.0.5, which is out of support
    statefulSet:
      spec:
        volumeClaimTemplates:
          - metadata:
              name: data-volume
            spec:
              accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
              storageClassName: <your_storage_class>
              resources:
                requests:
                  storage: 5Gi
          - metadata:
              name: logs-volume
            spec:
              accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
              storageClassName: <your_storage_class>
              resources:
                requests:
                  storage: 1Gi

managedMongo.spec is passed as is to the MongoDBCommunity resource; resources for the mongod and mongodb-agent containers go under statefulSet.spec.template.spec.containers.

docs.title: The marketplace
docs.text:
marketplace:
  enabled: true
  generatePasswords: false               # the Secrets above are created beforehand
  externalUrl: https://<your_marketplace_domain>
  tmForum:                               # the TMForum APIs, all served by tm-forum-api-svc
    catalog:           {host: tm-forum-api-svc, port: 8080, path: /tmf-api/productCatalogManagement/v4}
    inventory:         {host: tm-forum-api-svc, port: 8080, path: /tmf-api/productInventory/v4}
    ordering:          {host: tm-forum-api-svc, port: 8080, path: /tmf-api/productOrderingManagement/v4}
    billing:           {host: tm-forum-api-svc, port: 8080, path: /tmf-api/accountManagement/v4}
    usage:             {host: tm-forum-api-svc, port: 8080, path: /tmf-api/usageManagement/v4}
    party:             {host: tm-forum-api-svc, port: 8080, path: /tmf-api/party/v4}
    customer:          {host: tm-forum-api-svc, port: 8080, path: /tmf-api/customerManagement/v4}
    resources:         {host: tm-forum-api-svc, port: 8080, path: /tmf-api/resourceCatalog/v4}
    services:          {host: tm-forum-api-svc, port: 8080, path: /tmf-api/serviceCatalogManagement/v4}
    resourceInventory: {host: tm-forum-api-svc, port: 8080, path: /tmf-api/resourceInventoryManagement/v4}
    customerBill:      {host: tm-forum-api-svc, port: 8080, path: /tmf-api/customerBillManagement/v4}
  bizEcosystemChargingBackend:
    loglevel: info
    media:
      enabled: true                      # storage for the assets attached to offerings
      size: 2Gi
      storageClass: <your_storage_class>
  bizEcosystemLogicProxy:
    purchaseEnabled: true                # let consumers order offerings
    dataSpaceEnabled: true               # data space features in the portal
    ingress:
      enabled: true
      className: <your-ingress-class>    # add the annotations your ingress controller needs
      annotations:
        cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: "prod-issuer"
      hosts:
        - host: <your_marketplace_domain>
          paths: ["/"]
      tls:
        - secretName: <your_marketplace_domain>-tls
          hosts:
            - <your_marketplace_domain>

To create offerings whose data is exchanged over the Dataspace Protocol, also add BAE_LP_DSP_ENABLED=true to the logic proxy's environment, see Using the BAE Marketplace.

docs.title: Login with Verifiable Credentials
docs.text:
Users log in to the portal by presenting a Verifiable Credential to the provider's VCVerifier, which acts as the OpenID Connect provider of the BAE. Three pieces have to agree: the credential Keycloak issues, the service registered at the verifier, and the BAE's OIDC client.

1. The credential. The user presents a LegalPersonCredential with their e-mail and names, and their marketplace roles in a roles claim. The BAE builds the user's profile from it: the e-mail is mandatory (the user name is derived from it), and the roles must be named as the BAE expects them - seller to publish offerings, customer to order them, admin - or as set in marketplace.oauth.sellerrole, customerrole and adminrole. In Keycloak this is a credential scope with these mappers, and the roles are client roles of the provider's DID client assigned to the user - see the Keycloak guide for the credential configuration:

keycloak:
  realm:
    verifiableCredentials:
      legal-person-credential:
        attributes:
          format: "dc+sd-jwt"
          verifiable_credential_type: "LegalPersonCredential"
          credential_signing_alg: "ES256"
          credential_build_config.token_jws_type: "dc+sd-jwt"
          credential_build_config.sd_jwt.visible_claims: "iss,iat,nbf,exp,cnf,vct,status,roles,email"
        protocolMappers:
          - name: email-mapper
            protocol: oid4vc
            protocolMapper: oid4vc-user-attribute-mapper
            config:
              claim.name: email
              userAttribute: email
          - name: firstName-mapper
            protocol: oid4vc
            protocolMapper: oid4vc-user-attribute-mapper
            config:
              claim.name: firstName
              userAttribute: firstName
          - name: familyName-mapper
            protocol: oid4vc
            protocolMapper: oid4vc-user-attribute-mapper
            config:
              claim.name: familyName
              userAttribute: lastName
          - name: role-mapper
            protocol: oid4vc
            protocolMapper: oid4vc-target-role-mapper
            config:
              claim.name: roles
              clientId: <your_did>             # the client the marketplace roles are defined on

2. The service at the verifier. Register the marketplace as a service that requests that credential and passes its roles into the token:

decentralizedIam:
  vcAuthentication:
    vcverifier:
      registration:
        enabled: true
        services:
          - id: <your_did>                     # the BAE's OIDC client id
            defaultOidcScope: "openid learcredential"
            authorizationType: "FRONTEND_V2"
            oidcScopes:
              "openid learcredential":
                credentials:
                  - type: LegalPersonCredential
                    trustedParticipantsLists:
                      - <trust_anchor_tir_url>
                    trustedIssuersLists:
                      - http://trusted-issuers-list:8080
                    jwtInclusion:
                      enabled: true
                      fullInclusion: true      # the BAE builds the user's profile from the credential
                dcql:
                  credentials:
                    - id: legal-person-query
                      format: "dc+sd-jwt"
                      multiple: false
                      claims:
                        - id: roles-claim
                          path: [roles]
                      meta:
                        vct_values: [LegalPersonCredential]

Add it to the same registration.services list as the provider's other services: Helm replaces lists instead of merging them. A service that is already registered is not updated on upgrade; change it through the verifier's configuration API.

3. The BAE's OIDC client. The logic proxy uses its oidc-discover login, which reads the verifier's discovery document for that service:

marketplace:
  siop:
    enabled: false
  oauth:
    provider: oidc-discover
    oidc: true
    server: https://<your_verifier_domain>
    callbackPath: /auth/oidc-discover/callback
  bizEcosystemLogicProxy:
    additionalEnvVars:
      # this list replaces the chart's default one, which only disables tracing
      - name: OTEL_SDK_DISABLED
        value: "true"
      - name: BAE_LP_OAUTH2_CLIENT_ID
        value: <your_did>      # the id of the service registered above
      - name: BAE_LP_OAUTH2_CLIENT_SECRET
        value: unused          # the verifier does not check it
      - name: BAE_LP_OIDC_DISCOVERY_URI
        value: https://<your_verifier_domain>/services/<your_did>/.well-known/openid-configuration
      - name: BAE_LP_OIDC_SCOPES
        value: "openid learcredential"
      - name: BAE_LP_OAUTH2_NONCE
        value: "true"

The client id and secret go into the environment directly: setting oauth.clientId makes the chart read the secret from an oauthClientSecret key of the logic proxy's database Secret.

The marketplace chart can also log users in with SIOP (marketplace.siop). In its redirection mode (BAE_LP_SIOP_IS_REDIRECTION) the logic proxy signs its token requests with its own key, using the client id as key id, and the verifier resolves that key id as a DID to check them: the client id has to be the provider's DID and the key the DID's key. The OIDC login above has none of these constraints.

docs.title: Trusting a private CA
docs.text:
The logic proxy is a Node.js application: it calls the verifier over HTTPS and only trusts the public CAs. If the verifier's certificate comes from a private CA, mount the CA and point NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS to it, adding to the additionalEnvVars above:

marketplace:
  bizEcosystemLogicProxy:
    additionalEnvVars:
      # ... the variables of the previous section, and:
      - name: NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS
        value: /private-ca/ca.crt
    extraVolumeMounts:
      - name: private-ca
        mountPath: /private-ca
        readOnly: true
    extraContainerVolumes:
      - name: private-ca
        secret:
          secretName: <your_ca_secret>       # a Secret with the CA certificate under ca.crt
          items:
            - key: ca.crt
              path: ca.crt

Do not set NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0 instead: it disables certificate verification for every call the logic proxy makes. The local deployment in k3s/ uses it, but those values are meant for a test environment only.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text: Symptom Cause The portal ignores the data space settings DATASPACE_ENABLED is not read by the logic proxy; use bizEcosystemLogicProxy.dataSpaceEnabled: true The same variable twice in the logic proxy, or an upgrade fails with The order in patch list doesn't match $setElementOrder list A variable the chart already renders from a value - BAE_LP_PURCHASE_ENABLED, BAE_LP_DATASPACE_ENABLED, BAE_LP_SIOP_* - was also added to additionalEnvVars. Use the values Tracing settings disappear additionalEnvVars (logic proxy) and extraEnvVars (charging backend) replace the chart's lists, which hold the OTEL_* variables; keep OTEL_SDK_DISABLED bizEcosystemApis.tmForum in older examples The legacy name of tmForum; both work, tmForum wins A change to the BAE's service at the verifier has no effect The registration does not update a service that already exists; change it through the verifier's configuration API Orders are completed but nothing happens Contract management without organization.provider.role: seller The chart's MongoDB pod does not start (serviceaccounts "mongodb-database" not found) managedMongo.serviceAccount.create: false without a name, and the operator did not create its mongodb-database in the provider's namespace; see the operator

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• Do not publish the TMForum API or Scorpio. The BAE reaches them inside the cluster. If other participants need the TMForum API, publish it through APISIX, protected by the VCVerifier and ODRL policies, as the provider guide does for the data service.
  • The logic proxy's Party API answers without authentication (/party/individual returns the names and e-mail addresses of the registered individuals), and the catalog returns offerings that are still In design to anonymous users. Until the BAE restricts them, keep the portal's audience in mind and consider blocking those paths for anonymous callers at your ingress.
  • The marketplace chart sets no resource limits on its containers, and its wait-for-mongodb init container uses the outdated bitnamilegacy/mongodb:3.6.21 image.

docs.title: Installing and checking it
docs.text:
1. With the chart's MongoDB: install the MongoDB operator, once per cluster. With an existing MongoDB: create the marketplace's databases and users in it.
  2. Create the password Secrets in the provider's namespace, unless generatePasswords is used.
  3. Install or upgrade the connector with --wait and a generous --timeout, e.g. 30m. On a fresh install the charging backend and contract management restart a few times until the TMForum API and MongoDB are up; that is expected.
  4. Check that the logic proxy (<release>-biz-ecosystem-logic-proxy-0) and the charging backend are Running.
  5. Open https://<your_marketplace_domain>, log in with a wallet holding the LegalPersonCredential, and check that a user with the seller role can create an offering.

docs.title: Contract Management
docs.text:
Work in progress

Please note, that this document is currently being reworked for the usage of ODRL policies and does not contain the latest information

With the tmforum-api and the contract-management notification listener, the FIWARE Data Space Connector provides components to perform contract management based on the TMForum APIs.

Via the TMForum APIs, providers can create product specifications and offerings. Consumer organisations can register as a party and place product orders. In the case of a product order, the TMForum APIs will send a notification to the contract-management notification listener, which will create an entry at the Trusted Issuers List for the consumer organisation. Also compare to the flow descriptions of Consumer registration and Contract management.

docs.title: Authorization and authentication
docs.text:
The current implementation of the FIWARE Data Space Connector uses the decentralised version of the i4Trust framework with addtional support for http-path based decisions. This required, since the FIWARE Data Space Connector provides the TMForum APIs, instead of NGSI-LD APIs.

Work in progress

A more powerful security framework, also supporting attribute-based policies for the TMForum API, is currently build on top of the existing framework within the DOME Marketplace Project.

docs.title: Roles
docs.text:
The example-instance of the Data Space Connector supports two roles:

  • the PROVIDER, which is able to create Product Specifications and Offerings on the TMForum-API
  • the CONSUMER, which is able to order products through the api.
  • the LEGAL_REPRESENTATIVE, which is able to register an organization through the Parties API.

The roles are connected to policies inside the Authorization Registry. Those policies define the paths and operations available for each role at the TMForum API. In this case its:

PROVIDER: "GET","POST","PUT","DELETE" on all deployed TMForum APIs CONSUMER: "GET" on the ProductCatalogManagement-API and "GET","POST","PUT" on the ProductOrderingManagement-API LEGAL_REPRESENTATIVE: "GET", "POST" and "PUT" on the Parties-API

Warning

The hosted DSBA demo endpoints below are historical and are no longer available. Use the local deployment guide to run a current environment; adapt the example endpoints and users to your deployment.

docs.title: Credentials and Role-Assignment
docs.text:
The VerifiableCredentials containing the PROVIDER,CONSUMER and LEGAL_REPRESENTATIVE roles are issued through the standard mechanisms of the framework, e.g. by each individual participant. The example-instance of the Data Space Connector is in the role of an PROVIDER. Therefore, the user standard-employee(see the documentation for credentials) can request a NaturalPersonCredential at PacketDeliveries Keycloak (https://packetdelivery-kc.dsba.fiware.dev/realms/fiware-server/account/#/) with a compliant wallet (as of now, the demo-wallet.fiware.dev (https://demo-wallet.fiware.dev) can be used).

For the Consumer-Participant, two users are provided: - the legal-representative(see the documentation) with the role LEGAL_REPRESENTATIVE - the standard-user(see the documentation) with the role CONSUMER In order to get the credentials, use the HappyPets Keycloak (https://happypets-kc.dsba.fiware.dev/realms/fiware-server/account/#/).

Tip

The framework would allow users that have both roles already. We decided to split them in order to have a clear flow.

docs.title: Example flow
docs.text:
Work in progress

The Business API Ecosystem as a Marketplace solution build on top of the TMForum-APIs is currently beeing updated to the latest TMForum-APIs and the security framework. Once its finished, it can be used a Marketplace, including UI, for the Data Space Connector.

To provide a working example for Contract Management, using the Data Space Connector, a postman colletion is provided. It includes the following steps of the aquisition process:

Tip

Since frontend-solutions are still under construction, plain REST-calls are used for the flow. Since all calls require a valid JWT, the demo-portal (https://packetdelivery-portal.dsba.fiware.dev/) for the provider has a link to get a plain token in exchange for the Verifiable Credential. Log-in either as CONSUMER or PROVIDER (see Credentials and Role-Assignment) to get tokens.

  1. In order to have the consumer registered, it has to be created as an Organization through the TMForum Party-API. The registration needs to happen with a direct api-call to the Parties-API, with a token in Role LEGAL_REPRESENTATIVE: POST /organization

  2. Creating an offer as the PROVIDER (use a JWT retrieved for user standard-employee of PacketDelivery (https://packetdelivery-kc.dsba.fiware.dev/realms/fiware-server/account/#/)):

    1. Create the product specification
    2. Create the product offering

  3. Create a product order (e.g. buy the product) as the CONSUMER (use a JWT retrieved for user standard-user of HappyPets (https://happypets-kc.dsba.fiware.dev/realms/fiware-server/account/#/))

After the product was ordered, a notfication will be triggered towards the Contract Management Service. The service will use the information provided as part of the notification, to add the CONSUMER Organization as a Trusted Issuer to the Trusted Issuers List of PacketDelivery and therefore allow Happy Pets (as the CONSUMER Organization) to issue credentials to its customers to access Packet Deliveries (e.g. the PROVIDER) Services (see description of Service Usage in the Data Space).

docs.title: TMForum contract management example
docs.text: This is an example Postman collection providing requests to interact with the TMForum API for * Creating a product specification (by the provider) * Creating a product offering (by the provider) * Registering as party at the provider (creating an organization by the consumer) * Creating a product order (by the consumer)

docs.title: Service Interaction (M2M)
docs.text:
This document gives a detailed description of the steps in the Machine-To-Machine (M2M) service interaction flow for both client and server/provider side.

This flow applies to any kind of M2M interaction, e.g., for a service consumer's client to authenticate at the service provider or for a verifier component to authenticate at the trusted issuers registry.

docs.title: Client side
docs.text:
Before interacting with the server/provider, the client application first needs to obtain an access token from the /token endpoint of the server/provider.

Given a specific service endpoint https://<SERVICE_HOST>/<SERVICE_ENDPOINT> the client wants to interact with, a call to this endpoint without an Authorization header 

curl -X GET https://<SERVICE_HOST>/<SERVICE_ENDPOINT>
will most probably return an Unauthorized error.

In this case the client application needs to obtain an access (bearer) token at the /token endpoint of the server/provider. In order to obtain the address of this endpoint, the client application needs to call the well-known EBSI OpenID Provider Metadata endpoint in order to retrieve this endpoint. The address can be built with the known host of the server/provider: 

curl -X GET https://<SERVICE_HOST>/.well-known/openid-configuration

The response is a JSON object that should contain (at least) the following content: 

{
  "grant_types_supported": [
    "vp_token"
  ],
  "token_endpoint": "https://<SERVICE_TOKEN_HOST>/path/to/token",
}
One might also need to require specific entries in the field "scopes_supported", but this depends on the actual service. The actual endpoint to be used can be found in the parameter "token_endpoint".

In order to obtain the access token, the client application needs to send a vp_token to the server/provider's /token endpoint. The vp_token is a Signed Verifiable Presentation (VP) which includes the Verifiable Credential (VC) of the client/consumer and needs to be prepared by the client. Below is an example of the JWT content of such VP. * Header: 

{
  "typ": "JWT",
  "alg": "ES256",
  "kid": "did:ebsi:zdPj1GPXjfERXxXPE1YTYdJ#7j3TpaNdPNTOzOtouOOknlOLQk3JP-ykTfraWtY3GME"
}
* Payload: 
{
  "iss": "did:ebsi:zdPj1GPXjfERXxXPE1YTYdJ",
  "aud": "https://api-conformance.ebsi.eu/conformance/v3/auth-mock",
  "sub": "did:ebsi:zdPj1GPXjfERXxXPE1YTYdJ",
  "iat": 1589699260,
  "nbf": 1589699260,
  "exp": 1589699260,
  "nonce": "FgkeErf91kfl",
  "jti": "urn:uuid:0706061a-e2ca-4614-9de7-9c1451935f02",
  "vp": {
    "@context": [
      "https://www.w3.org/2018/credentials/v1"
    ],
    "id": "urn:uuid:0706061a-e2ca-4614-9de7-9c1451935f02",
    "type": [
      "VerifiablePresentation"
    ],
    "holder": "did:ebsi:zdPj1GPXjfERXxXPE1YTYdJ",
    "verifiableCredential": [
      "eyJ0eX....aEhOOXcifQ.eyJpj....J9fX0.9Drky3pj....lzTK3_-Q"
    ]
  } 
}
where "verifiableCredential" holds the actual VC.

The vp_token is then send to the EBSI Token compliant endpoint of the server/provider, together with additional parameters: 

curl -X POST 'https://<SERVICE_TOKEN_HOST>/path/to/token' \
-H 'Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' \
-H 'Accept: application/json' \
-d "vp_token=<SIGNED_VP_TOKEN>&grant_type=vp_token&presentation_submission=<PRESENTATION_SUBMISSION>&scope=<SCOPE>"
The parameter grant_type must be equal to vp_token and the parameter presentation_submission can be left empty at the moment. Depending on the actual service to be accessed one might need to request the token for a specific scope provided with the parameter scope. This would have been also listed in the Metadata of the service above.

As a response the client receives a JSON object containing the access token: 

{
  "access_token": "<ACCESS_TOKEN>",
  "token_type": "Bearer",
  "expires_in": 7200,
  "scope": "openid did_write",
  "id_token": "eyJ0eXAiOiJ....zI1NksifQ.eyJpYXQiOjE2N....VRURhZyJ9.YIdjUCinbG...Qyv14A"
}
The access token can be a simple string or a JWT containing information required by the service provider, e.g., containing the actual VC of the consumer.

The call to the service endpoint can now be retried with the access token being added to the Authorization header: 

curl -X GET https://<SERVICE_HOST>/<SERVICE_ENDPOINT> \
-H 'Authorization: Bearer <ACCESS_TOKEN>'

docs.title: Server side
docs.text: In the following, the two endpoints are described, which need to be implemented by a service provider in oder to be able to offer access to its services via the M2M flow.

docs.title: EBSI OpenID Provider Metadata Endpoint
docs.text:
On the server side, service providers need to implement the EBSI OpenID Provider Metadata endpoint. This is needed, so that consumers can obtain the actual /token endpoint needed to retrieve an access token before accessing the service in M2M flows.

Given a specific endpoint of the actual service provided, e.g., https://<SERVICE_HOST>/<SERVICE_ENDPOINT>, the well-known metadata endpoint should be accessible under https://<SERVICE_HOST>/.well-known/openid-configuration.

It should return a JSON object that should contain (at least) the following content: 

{
  "grant_types_supported": [
    "vp_token"
  ],
  "token_endpoint": "https://<SERVICE_TOKEN_HOST>/path/to/token",
}
One might also need to require specific entries in the field "scopes_supported", but this depends on the actual service. Also check the API specification linked above.

When using the VCVerifier component, this already implements such endpoint, providing the necessary data for the service endpoints configured in the Credentials Config Service component, and just needs a corresponding routing for the actual service host. The VCVerifier is providing the service-specific OpenID configuration under following endpoint: https://<VERIFIER_HOST>/services/<SERVICE_IDENTIFIER>/.well-known/openid-configuration.

docs.title: EBSI Token Endpoint
docs.text:
In order to be able to issue the access tokens, the service provider needs to implement the EBSI Token endpoint. Consumer applications are sending requests containing a vp_token to this endpoint, as described in the section Client side. The vp_token is a Signed Verifiable Presentation (VP) which includes the Verifiable Credential (VC) of the client/consumer.

When receiving a request with a vp_token, the following steps need to be performed: 1. Check that the contained VCs are of the required types for the provided scopes. 2. Verification of the signature of each of the required credentials. This depends on the DID method. 3. For each of the required credentials, check that these were issued by a trusted participant of the Data Space. This is done by a request against the Verifiable Data Registry of the Data Space which is implementing the EBSI Trusted Issuers Registry "Get an issuer" endpoint. 4. For each of the required credentials, check that these were issued by a trusted issuer stored at the provider's local Trusted Issuers List (meaning that the issuers have been granted rights to issue credentials of such type). The Trusted Issuers List also implements the EBSI Trusted Issuers Registry "Get an issuer" endpoint. An implementation can be found here. 5. When all checks were successful, return the response containing the access token. This access token should contain all the necessary information required by the actual service, especially the PDP component, to perform the authorization steps during interaction with the service.

When using the VCVerifier component, this already implements such endpoint, performing all the necessary verifications and validations when receiving the vp_token, and issuing JWT access tokens containing the VC which was included in the vp_token. The VCVerifier provides the /token endpoint under following URL: https://<VERIFIER_HOST>/token. Note that the /token endpoint in the VCVerifier is capable of handling both types of flows, H2M and M2M. It differentiates by the grant_type parameter. The implementation of the VCVerifier will return a JWT access token, containing the required VCs provided by the client in the request. This allows the PDP to extract all necessary information when performing the authorization steps during interaction with the service.

docs.title: Encoding and Padding
docs.text: Token send to the token endpoint require a base64url encoding without padding as described in Appendice C of RFC 7515.

docs.title: OID4VC Protocol Mappers — Keycloak 26.7.0
docs.text:
Feature flags required

keycloak.features.enabled must contain both oid4vc-vci and (since KC 26.4+) oid4vc-vci-preauth-code for the pre-authorized_code grant to work.

name field: A free-form identifier you choose to recognise the mapper within Keycloak. It has no functional impact — use any value that is meaningful to you (e.g. "my-email-mapper", "context-w3c", etc.). KC requires the name to be unique within a single ClientScope.

docs.title: Changes since 26.3.3
docs.text:
KC 26.4 redesigned the OID4VCI realm model (keycloak/keycloak#39768). The mapper-level changes that affect the examples below:

  • supportedCredentialTypes is removed from every mapper config. Mapper-to-credential association is now structural: each mapper belongs to exactly one ClientScope, and that ClientScope is the credential. To apply the same mapper logic to several VCs, declare the mapper once under each VC's protocolMappers list.
  • subjectProperty was renamed to claim.name on every mapper that had it (oid4vc-user-attribute-mapper, oid4vc-target-role-mapper, oid4vc-static-claim-mapper, oid4vc-generated-id-mapper, oid4vc-issued-at-time-claim-mapper).
  • oid4vc-subject-id-mapper uses claim.name plus userAttribute (the legacy subjectIdProperty is gone).
  • oid4vc-vc-type-mapper is deprecated. The Verifiable Credential Type is now a ClientScope attribute (vc.verifiable_credential_type) instead of a per-credential mapper.

The mappers themselves still live in the realm under keycloak.realm.verifiableCredentials.<name>.protocolMappers; the DSC chart renders one ClientScope (with protocol: "oid4vc") per VC entry.

docs.title: Table of Contents
docs.text:
• oid4vc-context-mapper
  • oid4vc-vc-type-mapper (deprecated)
  • oid4vc-subject-id-mapper
  • oid4vc-generated-id-mapper
  • oid4vc-user-attribute-mapper
  • oid4vc-target-role-mapper
  • oid4vc-static-claim-mapper
  • oid4vc-issued-at-time-claim-mapper

docs.title: oid4vc-context-mapper
docs.text:
Name: Credential Context Mapper

Assigns a @context entry to the Verifiable Credential. This is required by the W3C VC Data Model to define the semantic meaning of the credential's fields.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text: Property Label Type Default Description context Verifiable Credentials Context String https://www.w3.org/2018/credentials/v1 The context URL to assign to the credential.

docs.title: Example output
docs.text:
{
  "@context": [
    "https://www.w3.org/2018/credentials/v1",
    "https://example.org/my-custom-context/v1"
  ]
}

docs.title: Usage example
docs.text:
- name: context-mapper
  protocol: oid4vc
  protocolMapper: oid4vc-context-mapper
  config:
    context: https://www.w3.org/2018/credentials/v1

docs.title: oid4vc-vc-type-mapper (deprecated)
docs.text:
Warning

Deprecated in KC 26.4+. The Verifiable Credential Type is now a ClientScope attribute (vc.verifiable_credential_type), not a per-mapper setting. The DSC chart populates it from keycloak.realm.verifiableCredentials.<name>.attributes.verifiable_credential_type and also auto-derives vc.supported_credential_types from it (controlling the type array of JWT-VC JSON credentials). Do not declare this mapper in new realms; the section is kept here only for users migrating from 26.3.

Name: Credential Type Mapper

(Legacy) Assigned an additional type entry to the Verifiable Credential. Use the ClientScope attribute below instead.

docs.title: Replacement (10.x)
docs.text:
keycloak:
  realm:
    verifiableCredentials:
      EmployeeCredential:
        attributes:
          verifiable_credential_type: "EmployeeCredential"
          # supported_credential_types is auto-derived from the line above;
          # set it explicitly only if you need a different value in the
          # JWT-VC JSON `type` array than the SD-JWT `vct`.

docs.title: oid4vc-subject-id-mapper
docs.text:
Name: CredentialSubject ID Mapper

Assigns an id to the credentialSubject based on a configured user attribute (e.g. the user's DID, username, email, or the internal Keycloak user ID).

docs.title: Properties
docs.text: Property Label Type Default Description claim.name Subject ID Property Name String id The property name that will hold the subject ID inside credentialSubject. userAttribute User Attribute List did Which user attribute supplies the value. Allowed: did, username, email, id.

docs.title: Example output
docs.text:
{
  "credentialSubject": {
    "id": "did:example:ebfeb1f712ebc6f1c276e12ec21"
  }
}

docs.title: Usage example
docs.text:
- name: subject-id-mapper
  protocol: oid4vc
  protocolMapper: oid4vc-subject-id-mapper
  config:
    claim.name: id
    userAttribute: did

docs.title: oid4vc-generated-id-mapper
docs.text:
Name: Generated ID Mapper

Assigns a randomly generated ID to the credential subject. Unlike oid4vc-subject-id-mapper, this always generates a new ID — useful when you don't want to expose the user's actual identifier.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text: Property Label Type Default Description claim.name ID Property Name String id Name of the property to contain the generated id.

docs.title: Example output
docs.text:
{
  "credentialSubject": {
    "id": "urn:uuid:3d3c4b1a-9f2e-4c3b-8a1d-2f5e6b7c8d9e"
  }
}

docs.title: Usage example
docs.text:
- name: generated-id-mapper
  protocol: oid4vc
  protocolMapper: oid4vc-generated-id-mapper
  config:
    claim.name: id

docs.title: oid4vc-user-attribute-mapper
docs.text:
Name: User Attribute Mapper

Maps a standard Keycloak user attribute directly into the credentialSubject. This is one of the most commonly used mappers to include user profile data in a credential.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text: Property Label Type Default Description claim.name Attribute Property Name String — Property to add the user attribute to in the credential subject. userAttribute User Attribute List — The user attribute to be added to the credential subject. aggregateAttributes Aggregate Attributes Boolean false Should the mapper aggregate user attributes.

docs.title: Available userAttribute options
docs.text:
• username
  • locale
  • firstName
  • lastName
  • disabledReason
  • email
  • emailVerified

docs.title: Example output
docs.text:
{
  "credentialSubject": {
    "firstName": "Jane",
    "lastName": "Doe",
    "email": "jane.doe@example.com"
  }
}

docs.title: Usage example
docs.text:
💡 Create one mapper per attribute you want to include.

- name: user-email-mapper
  protocol: oid4vc
  protocolMapper: oid4vc-user-attribute-mapper
  config:
    claim.name: email
    userAttribute: email
    aggregateAttributes: "false"

docs.title: oid4vc-target-role-mapper
docs.text:
Name: Target-Role Mapper

Maps the roles assigned to a user into the credentialSubject, using the client ID as the target context. Useful for expressing authorization roles within a credential.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text: Property Label Type Default Description claim.name Roles Property Name String roles The property name to use in the credentialSubject for the roles. clientId Client ID String — Property to configure the client to get the roles from.

docs.title: Example output
docs.text:
{
  "credentialSubject": {
    "roles": [
      {
