docs.title: Per-component tracing
docs.text:
Each component can override the global tracing toggle independently via its own tracing.enabled key:

identityhub:
  tracing:
    enabled: true           # override global toggle
    serviceName: "my-identityhub"
    javaagent:
      enabled: true         # attach the OTEL Java agent via init container

fdsc-edc:
  tracing:
    serviceName: "my-fdsc-edc"

scorpio:
  tracing:
    serviceName: "scorpio"

keycloak:
  tracing:
    serviceName: "keycloak"

Components wired for tracing:

Component Mechanism Default service name IdentityHub OTEL Java agent (init container) + OTEL_* env vars identityhub fdsc-edc OTEL_* env vars via values.yaml fdsc-edc Keycloak OTEL_* env vars via subchart extraEnvVars keycloak Scorpio QUARKUS_OTEL_* env vars via subchart extraEnvVars scorpio tm-forum-api OTEL_* env vars via subchart additionalEnvVars tm-forum-api contract-management OTEL_* env vars via subchart deployment.additionalEnvVars contract-management marketplace OTEL_* env vars via subchart (logic-proxy) extraEnvVars marketplace decentralizedIam Forward-compatible passthrough (no runtime effect yet) —

docs.title: New values keys
docs.text:
The following top-level values.yaml keys are introduced:

Key Type Default Description tracing.enabled bool false Global on/off switch for OTEL tracing tracing.exporter.otlp.endpoint string "" OTLP endpoint (defaults to bundled collector) tracing.exporter.otlp.protocol string "grpc" OTLP protocol (grpc or http/protobuf) tracing.exporter.otlp.insecure bool true Disable TLS on the OTLP exporter tracing.sampler string "parentbased_traceidratio" Trace sampler name tracing.samplerArg string "1.0" Sampler argument (probability for ratio samplers) tracing.resourceAttributes map {} Extra resource attributes for all workloads tracing.propagators string "tracecontext,baggage" Propagators to use opentelemetry-collector.enabled bool false Toggle the bundled OTEL Collector subchart identityhub.tracing.enabled bool — Per-component tracing override identityhub.tracing.serviceName string "identityhub" OTEL service name for IdentityHub identityhub.tracing.javaagent.enabled bool true Attach the OTEL Java agent via init container

No existing values keys are modified or removed. Tracing is fully additive and opt-in.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text: Full documentation including architecture diagrams, backend integration examples, and troubleshooting is available at Distributed Tracing with OpenTelemetry.

docs.title: EDC / Dataspace Protocol production readiness
docs.text: The EDC part of the chart could be deployed but not operated: everything that keeps a participant's identity alive lived outside the chart, and several pieces broke on their own with no deployment involved. This release closes that.

docs.title: Participant provisioning is part of the chart
docs.text:
A deployed identityhub used to be inert - no participant context, no signing key in Vault, no credential - and the documented way to fix that was a curl sequence run from a workstation, which every real deployment reimplemented as a hand-written Job. identityhub.bootstrap now performs it in-cluster and idempotently, on install and on every upgrade.

Key Type Default Description identityhub.bootstrap.enabled bool false Provision the participant context from the chart identityhub.bootstrap.did string "" DID of this participant identityhub.bootstrap.keyAlias string key-1 Vault alias and DID fragment of the signing key identityhub.bootstrap.credentialServiceUrl string "" Public base URL of the DCP credential service identityhub.bootstrap.identityKey.secretName string "" Secret holding the identity private key identityhub.bootstrap.identityKey.algorithm string EC EC or RSA identityhub.bootstrap.stsClientSecret.existingSecret string "" Secret holding the STS shared secret identityhub.bootstrap.kidCheck.enabled bool false Verify the issuer signs with <did>#<keyAlias> identityhub.bootstrap.credential.secretName string "" Credential written by the vc-operator identityhub.bootstrap.rotation.enabled bool false Render the signing-key rotation Job

post-upgrade is part of the default hook and needs to stay there while Vault runs in dev mode: its storage is in-memory, so every Vault restart drops the signing key, the super-user credential and the STS client secret, and only a re-run restores them.

docs.title: The identityhub credential no longer goes stale on its own
docs.text:
The identityhub holds its own copy of the credential a connector presents, and nothing kept it in step: the vc-operator renewed the Secret while the identityhub went on presenting the previous credential until it expired, taking the DCP lane down with a Secret that looked perfectly healthy.

identityhub.credentialSync.enabled renders a sidecar in the identityhub pod that mirrors the Secret the vc-operator maintains into the identityhub's credential store, on issuance and on every renewal. It needs the Secret's name (identityhub.credentialSync.secretName) and the super-user api key in a Secret (identityhub.superuser.existingSecret).

The sidecar writes over localhost: the Identity API is component-internal, so the only thing that writes to it is the pod that owns the store. Obtaining and renewing the credential stays with the vc-operator, which never talks to the identityhub.

identityhub.bootstrap.credential.* is deprecated in favour of it and still read as a default: storing the credential is not a bootstrap concern, since a Job that only runs on install and upgrade leaves the copy stale after the first unattended renewal. The bootstrap Job no longer stores it.

Related: identityhub.credentialWatchdog.checkPeriodSeconds now exposes the identityhub's own watchdog, which re-requests expiring credentials from a DCP issuer service. It defaults to 0 (off), because the credentials here come from an OID4VCI issuer and there is no issuer service to ask; upstream defaults it to 60 seconds with a one-week renewal grace period, which for a credential that only lives a week means it is considered renewable from the moment it is issued.

Also consider raising renewBefore from the 5m default: five minutes leaves no room to notice a failure before the credential in use expires.

docs.title: Vault can keep its state across restarts
docs.text:
Key Type Default Description vault.hashicorp.existingSecret string "" Secret holding the Vault token, instead of a plaintext value vault.hashicorp.existingSecretTokenKey string token Key within that Secret vault.unattended.enabled bool false Persistent Vault, initialised and unsealed by the chart vault.unattended.autoUnseal bool true Unseal automatically; false means unsealing by hand vault.unattended.secretShares / .secretThreshold int 1 / 1 Shamir split of the master key vault.unattended.secretName string vault-unseal-keys Secret the unseal keys are written to vault.unattended.provisionToken bool true Mint the token the components use, and its ACL policy vault.unattended.tokenPeriod string 768h Period of that token; renewed by EDC in process vault.unattended.tokenPolicyName string dsc-connector Name of the policy created for it

vault.hashicorp.token is rendered into ConfigMaps in clear, so anyone able to read ConfigMaps in the namespace can read the credential that unlocks the participant's signing key. With existingSecret the identityhub receives it as EDC_VAULT_HASHICORP_TOKEN and the property is omitted from the ConfigMap entirely.

A Vault with persistent storage comes back sealed after every restart, so persistence alone is not enough; vault.unattended initialises an empty Vault once and unseals it whenever it finds it sealed, and mints the scoped token the components authenticate with.

The name is deliberate: this is not a production security posture. A Vault that unseals itself keeps its unseal keys in a Secret of the same namespace, so whoever can read Secrets there can open it. It is the right trade for demo and staging, where the alternative - dev mode - loses the participant's identity on every restart and does not put it back until the next deploy, because the bootstrap Job is a Helm hook and not a restart hook.

Production is autoUnseal: false: no unsealer is deployed, the operating organisation holds the key shares, and a quorum unseals on every start. That step cannot be automated away. Both variants, including the one-off init and the per-start procedure, are in the production guide.

vault.unattended.enabled refuses to render next to vault.server.dev.enabled rather than quietly doing nothing.

docs.title: Rotating the signing key
docs.text:
identityhub.bootstrap.rotation replaces the identity key while keeping the same Vault alias and the same DID fragment, which is what keeps the Keycloak realm out of it - signing_key_id is a ClientScope attribute and cannot be changed by automation on an existing realm.

There is no overlap window. The moment the key is replaced, everything signed with the previous one under that fragment stops verifying, credentials already in wallets included, so re-issuance is part of the operation. The Job is opt-in and never a Helm hook. The runbook is in the production guide.

Note also that cert-manager's privateKey.rotationPolicy defaults to Always since cert-manager 1.18, i.e. renewing a certificate generates a new key, which invalidates the published DID document. Declare rotationPolicy: Never explicitly for the identity key.

docs.title: Changed defaults
docs.text:
Key Old New Why fdsc-edc.common.config.tmfExtension.enabled true false It shipped enabled with seven empty addresses, and TMFConfig converts them with URI.create(...).toURL() at boot, so the default configuration aborted startup with URI is not absolute. Enabling it requires all seven. fdsc-edc.common.config.oid4vp.trustAll true false Disabling TLS verification is not a safe default. fdsc-edc.common.config.edc.log.level DEBUG INFO DEBUG logs every DSP message, token contents included. registration.annotations["helm.sh/hook"] post-install post-install,post-upgrade With post-install only, a release that already exists never re-registers, so nothing added to registration.issuer after the first install ever reached the trusted-issuers list.

Required action: if you relied on tmfExtension being enabled by default, set fdsc-edc.common.config.tmfExtension.enabled: true explicitly. The k3s/dsp-*.yaml values in this repository were updated the same way.

This matters beyond TMForum, and the symptom points nowhere near it. The extension is what registers the connector's ObjectMapper, imperatively, at the end of TMFContractNegotiationExtension.initialize() - which returns early when disabled. Several extensions inject one, so with TMF off the boot dies at whichever of them comes first, usually OID4VPExtension:

No default provider for required injection point Field "objectMapper"
  of type [class com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper]

Any deployment using the OID4VP lane needs tmfExtension.enabled: true and all seven addresses.

docs.title: Fixes
docs.text:
• vc.expiry_in_seconds and vc.refresh_interval_in_seconds are kept in sync. The admin console shows the first while the issued exp comes from the second, so setting only one produced credentials expiring at a completely different time than the console claimed - with Keycloak's default, a week instead of whatever was configured. Setting neither still leaves Keycloak's defaults alone.
  • vc.signing_key_id defaults to the key id the DID document publishes when the identityhub serves that document. Keycloak otherwise defaults it to the bare DID, which is not resolvable there, and issuance fails with No key for id '<did>' and algorithm ... available.
  • The trusted-issuers registration script treats a 409 as success. It used curl -f, so an already-registered issuer failed the Job - which is why making it run on upgrade required this fix first.
  • identityhub.customCaCerts works. The deployment mounted an empty emptyDir over the JVM truststore and referenced a ConfigMap nothing created, so declaring extra CAs replaced the whole truststore with nothing. An init container now imports them into a copy of it.
  • identityhub.customCaCertsFrom takes CAs from Secrets and ConfigMaps that already exist, so a cert-manager Secret can be pointed at instead of having its PEM copied into values. Sources are merged with a projected volume and a deployment that uses only this key renders no ConfigMap at all. Secrets default to ca.crt: mounting a kubernetes.io/tls Secret whole would put tls.key in the pod and fail the import.
  • identityhub.logging.persistence is gone. It mounted a claim that nothing created, so enabling it produced a pod that could never be scheduled. Rather than add the missing claim, the option was removed: the file handler writes to an emptyDir and the console handler is what feeds the cluster's log stack, which is where logs belong.
  • The identityhub service exposes the accounts port (8085) that the deployment opens, so the STS Accounts API is reachable in-cluster.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: helm unittest gained suites covering the bootstrap, the credential-sync sidecar, the unattended Vault surface and the holder key id cross-check, and .github/scripts/eval.sh now renders each chart's ci/*-values.yaml in addition to its defaults. Until now nothing in the EDC lane was linted or schema-validated at all, because it is all disabled by default.

docs.title: Consent management
docs.text:
The connector can now record and enforce consent (ISO/IEC TS 27560) on a data path, opt-in via the consent maven profile. A data subject's personal data is released to a consumer only while that subject has a granted consent for it.

Three components carry it, each deployed from its own published FIWARE chart:

component chart runs at consent-manager oci://quay.io/fiware/helm-charts/consent-manager the authority (trust-anchor release) consent-facade oci://quay.io/fiware/helm-charts/consent-facade the authority, plus a provider-local instance consent-owner-resolver oci://quay.io/fiware/helm-charts/consent-owner-resolver the provider

Enforcement itself is an APISIX external plugin (consent-filter) on the provider's mp-data-service-consent route: OPA authorizes the request on the presented credential, then the plugin asks the owner-resolver whose data was returned and checks that owner's consent at the consent-manager - so the decision is made from the data, not from whoever requested it.

Participants and data subjects authenticate over OID4VP throughout; no component holds a participant client secret, and the shared consent key is injected by the authority's APISIX facade rather than handed to callers.

See Consent Management for the architecture, the enabling overlays and two end-to-end walkthroughs.

docs.title: contract-management 3.3.12 requires trusted-issuers-list >= 0.9.0
docs.text:
contract-management now registers the credentials of a newly onboarded participant through PUT /issuer/{did}/credential?scope=<product-order-id>, an endpoint that only exists from trusted-issuers-list 0.9.0 on. Against an older list the call answers 404, the issuer keeps its old credential set, and the participant's token exchange fails with forbidden_claim_or_value at the verifier - for example an OperatorCredential that was never allowed for the issuer.

Both charts therefore ship a list that serves it:

chart dependency version list data-space-connector decentralized-iam 2.1.19 -> 2.1.21 0.8.1 -> 0.9.1 (via vc-authentication 1.3.7) trust-anchor trusted-issuers-list 0.18.4 -> 0.18.7 0.8.1 -> 0.9.1

The decentralized-iam bump also raises vcverifier from 6.15.1 to 6.21.0 and odrl-authorization stays at 2.4.1. If you run the list outside the chart (trusted-issuers-list.enabled: false), raise your own deployment to >= 0.9.0 before upgrading.

docs.title: Release 11.x.x
docs.text:
Version 11.x.x of the Data Space Connector replaces the consent-manager of the consent management scenario. Changes will be listed below, together with the required actions for migration.

Only deployments that use consent management are affected: the data-space-connector chart loses one value that no template read, while the breaking changes are in the trust-anchor chart and in the consent-filter plugin.

docs.title: 11.0.0 — consent management moves to dsc-consent-manager
docs.text:
The consent-manager of the consent management scenario is replaced: the Prometheus-X service (Node, MongoDB, a shared consent key, APISIX facade routes at the authority) gives way to dsc-consent-manager (Java, PostgreSQL), which validates the JWT of the authority's VCVerifier on every call. See ADR 0008 and Consent Management, which also describes the migration.

The data-space-connector chart only loses one value: consentManagement.enabled, which no template ever read. The provider side is the consent-facade and consent-owner-resolver subcharts plus the consent-plugin on the provider's APISIX, each with its own enabled. Drop the key from your values - values.schema.json rejects what the chart does not declare. A provider that does not use consent management has nothing to do.

The breaking changes for consent users are elsewhere:

  • trust-anchor chart 2.0.0 deploys dsc-consent-manager 0.1.0 under the unchanged consent-manager key, pinned to image 0.0.3 with consent-manager.deployment.image.tag because that chart's appVersion is still 0.0.1. The pin is required, not cosmetic. Before 0.0.3:
  • 0.0.1 answers every POST /v1/privacy-notices/by-contract with a 502 against a contract service that keeps only bilateral contracts - which the consent-facade is, since it answers the ecosystem endpoint with 501;
  • it cannot be exempted from a global HTTP proxy at all, because a client set to proxy-type: DIRECT inherits the global proxy address and then fails every request;
  • a contract party was identified by the participant identifier alone, while the consent-facade's /verify - the lookup the owner-resolver makes to find the governing contract - matches only the participants' self-description URLs. One agreement can carry only one form in provider-id/consumer-id, so notice generation and the consent gate could not both work: with DIDs every gated read was denied, with URLs generation answered 404 No active participant is registered under '<url>'. 0.0.3 accepts either name (ADR-0017 of dsc-consent-manager), and the agreements this deployment writes carry the self-description URLs, as contract-management already did.

Drop the pin once the dependency moves to a chart whose appVersion is 0.0.3 or newer. - The consent MongoDB and its values are gone. The service stores its data in the chart's Zalando managedPostgres, under a user and database both fixed to consent_manager. External Postgres is not supported. - The consent key is gone. Callers authenticate with a JWT of the VCVerifier service consent-manager, set with consent-manager.identityProviders.primary. - A setup Job (consentManagement.setup) copies the database credentials into consent-manager-env and generates the receipt signing key in consent-manager-signing-keys, once; it never rotates them. The database itself is created by the Zalando operator from managedPostgres.config.databases, on a fresh cluster and on an existing volume alike. consentManagement.setup.resources sizes its containers, and its ServiceAccount and RBAC can be managed outside the chart with consentManagement.setup.serviceAccount.create / .name and consentManagement.setup.rbac.create. - SMTP credentials come from consentManagement.smtp.existingSecret. - The consent-manager's NetworkPolicy admits its management port (9090) to consentManagement.networkPolicy.metricsScrapers only. Enabling consent-manager.serviceMonitor without listing the scraping Prometheus there drops every scrape. - The chart fails on the removed values: managedMongo, consentManagement.mongo, consent-manager.mongo, consent-manager.secret.consentKey, consent-manager.externalIdp, consent-manager.appEndpoint, consent-manager.contractService and consent-manager.secrets.smtpUser/smtpPassword. - The provider's consent route needs consent-filter plugin 1.0.0, which speaks only the /v1 API, so the image and the route config change together. consent_api_url points at the consent-manager directly; there is no authority facade in between. consent_api_host and consent_key are removed. check_mode, consumer_claim, require_purpose and require_contract are new. Provider and consumer must both be registered participants at the consent-manager.

Consents stored in MongoDB are not migrated. Data subjects have to grant them again under the new service.

docs.title: Release 8.x.x
docs.text: Version 8.x.x of the Data Space Connector contains a number of new features and improvements. They will be listed below, together with required actions for migration.

docs.title: Marketplace Integration
docs.text: In order to provide a frontend for the marketplace functionality, the BAE Marketplace(https://github.com/FIWARE-TMForum/Business-API-Ecosystem) was integrated into the Data Space Connector. See Marketplace Integration for more details.

docs.title: Keycloak Update to 26.3.2
docs.text:
Keycloak has some fundamental changes in the configuration of Verifiable Credentials Issuance and in its support of the OID4VCI protocol. Increased support is still a major work-item in Keycloak, thus more changes will come soon.

Required action:

The configuration of the realm needs to be updated to the new format of keyclaok. See attributes, client-scopes and clients section of the consumer-example config as an example

docs.title: TMForum API update
docs.text:
To better support Marketplace integration and contract negotiation, the TMForum API was updated to 1.3.6.

If the TMForum API was not used before, nothing has to be done.

Required action: If the connector instance already contains data from TMForum <1.0.0, a data migration needs to be executed: https://github.com/FIWARE/tmforum-api/tree/main/data-migrator

docs.title: Local Deployment
docs.text: In order to better support demo-scenarios integrating end-users and frontends, the local deployment now contains an additional proxy to provide access to the services. See https://github.com/FIWARE/data-space-connector/blob/main/doc/deployment-integration/local-deployment/LOCAL.md#local-deployment and https://github.com/FIWARE/data-space-connector/blob/main/doc/MARKETPLACE_INTEGRATION.md#demo-usage for more details.

docs.title: ODRL-PAP
docs.text:
The ODRL-PAP was updated to 1.0.2, in order to better support the accessibility of policies(e.g. query-by-id - see ODRL-PAP API). It also requires policies to contain a "odrl:uid" now, to be compliant with the odrl-spec.

Required actions:

Update all policies to include a "odrl:uid"(see spec)

docs.title: Verifier & Credentials-Config-Service update for EUDI-Wallet compatibility
docs.text:
In order to be compliant with the current EUDI-Wallet(https://github.com/eu-digital-identity-wallet), the Verifier has various updates in its OID4VP support:

* presentationDefinition: following the OID4VP spec, the specification of "presentationDefinition" is now supported. See [registration in the provider.yaml](https://github.com/FIWARE/data-space-connector/blob/main/k3s/provider.yaml#L148-L189) as an example
* jwtInclusion: in order to reduce the size of created JWT-Tokens and flexibility in their structure, the inclusion of VC Claims into the JWT can now be configured. See [Credential-Config-Service API](https://github.com/FIWARE/credentials-config-service/blob/main/api/credentials-config-service.yaml#L225-L253)
* requestMode: To improve integration with applications and OID4VP compliance, the verifier now supports(in addition to "urlEncoded") the request modes "byValue" and "byReference". See [VCVerifier](https://github.com/FIWARE/VCVerifier?tab=readme-ov-file#request-modes) for more details.  
* request signing: The verifier now supports signing request objects sent to the wallet. See [Verifier Configuration](https://github.com/FIWARE/VCVerifier?tab=readme-ov-file#configuration) - "verifier.clientIdentification"
* horizontal scaling: in order to support horizontal scaling, the a Key for signing the JWT's can be provided to the instances. See [Verifier Configuration](https://github.com/FIWARE/VCVerifier?tab=readme-ov-file#configuration) - "verifier.keyAlgorithm", "verifier.generateKey" and "verifier.keyPath"

Required actions: * update Verifier configuration - see provider.yaml - vcverifier as example * update Credentials-Configuration - see provider.yaml - credentials-config-service as example

docs.title: Wallet Integration
docs.text: For various Use-Cases, the integration of EUDI Wallet - compatible End-User Wallets is required. The new version of the Data Space Connector contains a local runnable example, demonstrating the integration with the current Reference Implementation. See Marketplace integration - The Wallet for more.

docs.title: Release 9.x.x
docs.text: Version 9.x.x of the Data Space Connector contains a number of breaking changes and improvements. They will be listed below, together with required actions for migration.

docs.title: Decentralized-IAM Integration
docs.text:
All IAM and authorization components are now consolidated under a new decentralized-iam umbrella chart. The following top-level chart dependencies have been removed and are now managed under decentralizedIam:

Removed (8.5.2) New location (9.0.0) mysql N/A — replaced by postgres-operator postgresql (for auth/PAP/Keycloak/IdentityHub) N/A — replaced by postgres-operator postgis (for Scorpio) N/A — replaced by postgres-operator vcverifier decentralizedIam.vcAuthentication.vcverifier credentials-config-service decentralizedIam.vcAuthentication.credentials-config-service trusted-issuers-list decentralizedIam.vcAuthentication.trusted-issuers-list dss decentralizedIam.vcAuthentication.dss odrl-pap decentralizedIam.odrlAuthorization.odrl-pap apisix (+ OPA sidecar) decentralizedIam.odrlAuthorization.apisix

Required action:

Replace all individual IAM component configurations in your values file with the new decentralizedIam structure:

decentralizedIam:
  enabled: true
  vcAuthentication:
    trusted-issuers-list: ...
    vcverifier: ...
    credentials-config-service: ...
    dss: ...
  odrlAuthorization:
    apisix: ...
    odrl-pap: ...
    opa: ...
    tpp: ...

The following top-level values keys are no longer valid and must be removed:

authentication.*
dataplane.*
didJson.*
mysql.*
postgresql.*  (top-level)
postgis.*
vcverifier.*  (top-level)
credentials-config-service.*  (top-level)
trusted-issuers-list.*  (top-level)
dss.*  (top-level)
odrl-pap.*  (top-level)
apisix.*  (top-level)
opa.*  (top-level)
tpp.*  (top-level)

docs.title: Zalando postgres-operator
docs.text:
The chart no longer ships individual Bitnami PostgreSQL or MySQL instances for auth components. Instead, it uses the Zalando postgres-operator to create and manage a single PostgreSQL cluster with all required databases and users.

The vc-authentication subchart (part of decentralized-iam) includes postgres-operator 1.15.1 as a direct dependency. You have two options:

Option A — Let the chart install the operator (recommended for new installations):

The postgres-operator chart ships its CRDs in its crds/ directory, so Helm installs them automatically on helm install:

decentralizedIam:
  vcAuthentication:
    postgres-operator:
      enabled: true   # default: true

Helm upgrade caveat

Helm only installs CRDs on helm install, not on helm upgrade. If the postgres-operator CRDs change in a future version, apply them manually before upgrading: 

kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/zalando/postgres-operator/refs/heads/master/charts/postgres-operator/crds/postgresqls.yaml
kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/zalando/postgres-operator/refs/heads/master/charts/postgres-operator/crds/operatorconfigurations.yaml
kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/zalando/postgres-operator/refs/heads/master/charts/postgres-operator/crds/postgresteams.yaml

Option B — Use an externally managed operator:

decentralizedIam:
  vcAuthentication:
    postgres-operator:
      enabled: false

The managedPostgres section controls the postgresql.acid.zalan.do CRD that defines the actual cluster:

decentralizedIam:
  vcAuthentication:
    managedPostgres:
      enabled: true
      config:
        teamId: "dsc"   # cluster service will be named: postgres
        numberOfInstances: 1
        postgresql:
          version: "16"
        volume:
          size: 1Gi
        users:
          admin: [superuser, createdb]
          til: [createdb]
          ccs: [createdb]
          pap: [createdb]
          keycloak: [createdb]
          ih: [createdb]
          issuer: [createdb]
        databases:
          tildb: til
          ccsdb: ccs
          papdb: pap
          keycloakdb: keycloak
          ih: ih
          issuer: issuer

Required action:

All database secrets and hostnames have changed. The operator auto-generates one Kubernetes Secret per user following the pattern {username}.postgres.credentials.postgresql.acid.zalan.do. Update all secret references:

Component Old secret / key New secret / key TIL, CCS authentication-database-secret / mysql-root-password postgres.postgres.credentials.postgresql.acid.zalan.do / password ODRL-PAP, Keycloak, Scorpio database-secret / postgres-admin-password postgres.postgres.credentials.postgresql.acid.zalan.do / password IdentityHub database-secret / postgres-admin-password ih.postgres.credentials.postgresql.acid.zalan.do / password

Database hostnames and names have also changed:

Component Old host / DB New host / DB TIL, CCS authentication-mysql / tildb, ccsdb postgres / tildb, ccsdb ODRL-PAP postgresql / pap postgres / papdb Keycloak postgresql / keycloak postgres / keycloakdb Scorpio data-service-postgis postgres IdentityHub (empty) postgres

Note: the ODRL-PAP database was renamed from pap to papdb. Migrate any existing policy data before upgrading.

docs.title: TIL and CCS: MySQL replaced by PostgreSQL
docs.text:
trusted-issuers-list and credentials-config-service previously used MySQL. They now use PostgreSQL. Liquibase migrations will run against the new databases on first startup.

Required action:

If you have existing data in the MySQL databases (tildb, ccsdb), migrate it to the new PostgreSQL instance using a tool such as pgloader before upgrading.

Update the database dialect in your values:

decentralizedIam:
  vcAuthentication:
    trusted-issuers-list:
      database:
        dialect: POSTGRES
        host: postgres
        port: 5432
        username: postgres
        existingSecret:
          name: postgres.postgres.credentials.postgresql.acid.zalan.do
          key: password
        name: tildb

docs.title: Verifier: built-in credentials config server (credentials-config-service no longer required)
docs.text:
The vcverifier now ships a built-in config server that reads credential configurations directly from the same PostgreSQL database previously managed by credentials-config-service. Deploying credentials-config-service as a separate component is therefore no longer necessary.

Required action:

1. Configure the verifier's database connection using the same database that credentials-config-service was pointing to (ccsdb), and enable the built-in config server:

decentralizedIam:
  vcAuthentication:
    vcverifier:
      deployment:
        verifier:
          database:
            persistence: true
            dialect: POSTGRES
            username: postgres
            existingSecret:
              enabled: true
              name: postgres.postgres.credentials.postgresql.acid.zalan.do
              key: password
            host: postgres
            port: 5432
            name: ccsdb
        configServer:
          enabled: true
        configRepo:
          configEndpoint: ""

Note that configRepo.configEndpoint must be set to an empty string so the verifier uses the built-in config server instead of an external credentials-config-service endpoint.

2. Disable credentials-config-service:

decentralizedIam:
  vcAuthentication:
    credentials-config-service:
      enabled: false

docs.title: APISIX: Bitnami chart replaced by Apache chart
docs.text:
The APISIX chart dependency has changed from the Bitnami chart to the official Apache APISIX chart:

8.5.2 9.0.0 Chart bitnami/apisix 6.0.0 apisix/apisix 2.13.0 Repository oci://registry-1.docker.io/bitnamicharts https://apache.github.io/apisix-helm-chart Location Top-level dependency decentralizedIam.odrlAuthorization.apisix

Required action:

All Bitnami-specific APISIX values are invalid in 9.0.0. The Bitnami chart had a significantly different structure (controlPlane, dataPlane, etcd sections, bitnamilegacy images, extra volumes for routes and OPA). If you had custom APISIX routes or OPA configuration, translate them to the Apache APISIX Helm chart format under decentralizedIam.odrlAuthorization.apisix.

docs.title: Keycloak: keystore password configuration changed
docs.text:
In 8.5.2, the keystore password was injected into Keycloak via the STORE_PASS environment variable reading from the kc-keystore Kubernetes secret. This has been removed.

In 9.0.0 the keystore credentials are configured directly in values and rendered into the Keycloak realm configuration. Two approaches are supported:

Option A — did:elsi (top-level elsi section): 

elsi:
  enabled: true
  did: did:elsi:myDid
  keyAlgorithm: EC
  storePath: /path/to/keystore.p12
  storePassword: my-store-password
  keyAlias: my-key-alias
  keyPassword: my-key-password

Option B — generic signing key (keycloak.signingKey): 

keycloak:
  signingKey:
    storePath: /path/to/keystore.p12
    storePassword: my-store-password
    keyAlias: my-key-alias
    keyPassword: my-key-password
    keyAlgorithm: EC

Required action:

The passwords are rendered inline into the realm ConfigMap. To avoid plain-text passwords in your values file, use ${ENV_VAR} placeholders and load them from a Kubernetes secret via keycloak.extraEnvVars:

elsi:
  storePassword: "${STORE_PASS}"
  keyPassword: "${KEY_PASS}"

keycloak:
  extraEnvVars:
    - name: STORE_PASS
      valueFrom:
        secretKeyRef:
          name: my-keystore-secret
          key: store-password
    - name: KEY_PASS
      valueFrom:
        secretKeyRef:
          name: my-keystore-secret
          key: key-password

The same pattern applies to Option B using keycloak.signingKey.

docs.title: Keycloak realm: structured YAML format for realm properties
docs.text: The following keycloak.realm properties now accept native YAML structures in addition to the legacy raw JSON string format. The string format remains fully supported for backwards compatibility.

docs.title: attributes — dictionary
docs.text:
# OLD (string)
keycloak:
  realm:
    attributes: |
    "myKey": "myValue",
    "anotherKey": "anotherValue"'

# NEW (map)
keycloak:
  realm:
    attributes:
      myKey: myValue
      anotherKey: anotherValue

docs.title: clientRoles — dictionary (key → list of role objects)
docs.text:
# OLD (string)
keycloak:
  realm:
    clientRoles: |
      "my-client": [{"name": "my-role"}],
      "second-client": [{"name": "my-role-2"}]

# NEW (map)
keycloak:
  realm:
    clientRoles:
      my-client:
        - name: my-role
      second-client:
        - name: my-role-2

docs.title: users — list
docs.text:
# OLD (string)
keycloak:
  realm:
    users: |
    {"username": "admin", "enabled": true},
    {"username": "test", "enabled": true}

# NEW (list)
keycloak:
  realm:
    users:
      - username: admin
        enabled: true
      - username: test
        enabled: true

docs.title: clients — list
docs.text:
# OLD (string)
keycloak:
  realm:
    clients: '{"clientId": "my-client", "enabled": true}'

# NEW (list)
keycloak:
  realm:
    clients:
      - clientId: my-client
        enabled: true

docs.title: clientScopes — list
docs.text:
# OLD (string)
keycloak:
  realm:
    clientScopes: |
    {"name": "my-scope", "protocol": "openid-connect"},
    {"name": "my-scope2", "protocol": "openid-connect"}

# NEW (list)
keycloak:
  realm:
    clientScopes:
      - name: my-scope
        protocol: openid-connect
      - name: my-scope-2
        protocol: openid-connect

docs.title: Keycloak realm: default values split into extensible properties
docs.text:
Several realm properties that previously shipped hardcoded defaults have been split into a default* key (chart-managed defaults) and an extra* or override key (user additions). This allows extending the defaults without redefining them entirely.

Property Default key Extension key Type Realm roles defaultRealmRoles extraRealmRoles list Groups defaultGroups extraGroups list Client scopes defaultClientScopes clientScopes list Default default client scopes defaultDefaultClientScopes extraDefaultClientScopes list Default optional client scopes defaultOptionalClientScopes extraOptionalClientScopes list Client roles defaultClientRoles clientRoles dict Clients defaultClients clients list Key providers defaultKeyProviders extraKeyProviders list

Example — adding an extra realm role without redefining the defaults:

# OLD — had to repeat all existing roles plus the new one
keycloak:
  realm:
    realmRoles: '{"name": "default-roles-provider"}, {"name": "offline_access"}, {"name": "my-custom-role"}'

# NEW — only define what you add
keycloak:
  realm:
    extraRealmRoles:
      - name: my-custom-role

Example — adding an extra client scope:

keycloak:
  realm:
    clientScopes:
      - name: my-scope
        protocol: openid-connect
        attributes:
          include.in.token.scope: "true"

docs.title: Keycloak realm: automatic optionalClientScopes population for default clients
docs.text:
The chart now automatically populates optionalClientScopes for each client defined under keycloak.realm.defaultClients. The injected scopes are derived from all three sources:

  • keycloak.realm.defaultClientScopes — chart-managed default scopes
  • keycloak.realm.clientScopes — user-defined extra scopes
  • Scopes auto-generated from keycloak.realm.verifiableCredentials

A scope is only added to optionalClientScopes if it is not already present in that client's defaultClientScopes, avoiding duplicates across both scope lists.

docs.title: Keycloak realm: dedicated verifiableCredentials property
docs.text:
A new keycloak.realm.verifiableCredentials property allows declaring each verifiable credential as a self-contained block. Each entry combines three concerns in one place: the VC realm attributes, the client scope that Keycloak exposes for that credential, and its protocol mappers.

Tip

Recommended over clientScopes and attributes for VC configuration

Keycloak versions after 26.3 will introduce a breaking change in how verifiable credentials are configured: VC attributes will no longer be stored as plain realm attributes. Declaring VCs through verifiableCredentials ensures the chart can handle that transition transparently. Migrating existing VC client scopes from clientScopes to verifiableCredentials is recommended — it avoids duplicates and keeps the full VC definition in one place. If you prefer to keep managing the client scope manually under clientScopes, set clientScope.create: false to prevent the chart from generating it automatically.

Each entry supports the following fields:

Field Description attributes Map of VC attributes, flattened as vc.{id}.{attr} into the realm attributes. Object values are serialized as JSON strings automatically. clientScope.create Whether to auto-generate a client scope for this VC. Defaults to true. Set to false to skip creation. protocolMappers List of protocol mappers to attach to the generated client scope. See oid4vc-protocol-mappers.md for available mappers and their configuration. 
keycloak:
  realm:
    verifiableCredentials:
      my-credential:
        attributes:
          credential_signing_alg_values_supported: "ES256"
          format: "vc+sd-jwt"
          scope: "MyCredential"
          vct: "MyCredential"
          credential_build_config.signing_algorithm: "ES256"
          credential_build_config.token_jws_type: "vc+sd-jwt"
          credential_build_config.visible_claims: "roles,email"
          # object values are automatically serialized as JSON strings
          credential_build_config.proof_types_supported:
            jwt:
              proof_signing_alg_values_supported:
                - ES256
        clientScope:
          create: true   # default, can be omitted
        protocolMappers:
          - name: email-mapper
            protocol: oid4vc
            protocolMapper: oid4vc-user-attribute-mapper
            config:
              subjectProperty: email
              userAttribute: email
              supportedCredentialTypes: MyCredential
          - name: role-mapper
            protocol: oid4vc
            protocolMapper: oid4vc-target-role-mapper
            config:
              subjectProperty: roles
              clientId: did:web:my-did.example.org
              supportedCredentialTypes: MyCredential

The attributes block produces the following realm attributes (merged last, taking precedence over keycloak.realm.attributes):

{
  "vc.my-credential.credential_signing_alg_values_supported": "ES256",
  "vc.my-credential.format": "vc+sd-jwt",
  "vc.my-credential.scope": "MyCredential",
  "vc.my-credential.vct": "MyCredential",
  "vc.my-credential.credential_build_config.signing_algorithm": "ES256",
  "vc.my-credential.credential_build_config.token_jws_type": "vc+sd-jwt",
  "vc.my-credential.credential_build_config.visible_claims": "roles,email",
  "vc.my-credential.credential_build_config.proof_types_supported": "{\"jwt\":{\"proof_signing_alg_values_supported\":[\"ES256\"]}}"
}

When clientScope.create is true (the default), the chart also generates a client scope entry using attributes.scope as the name and attaches the protocolMappers. This scope is automatically added to the optionalClientScopes of each default client (skipping any already present in that client's defaultClientScopes).

Migration: if you previously declared VC-related client scopes under keycloak.realm.clientScopes, move them to verifiableCredentials and remove the duplicate entries from clientScopes to avoid the scope appearing twice in the realm.

docs.title: did-helper: alias changed and new certificate serving capability
docs.text:
The did-helper chart alias and condition have changed:

8.5.2 9.0.0 Alias did-helper did Condition did-helper.enabled did.enabled

did-helper is a lightweight server that generates and serves a DID document at /.well-known/did.json. It supports two modes for key material:

  • generateKey (default): Generates a new EC (or RSA) key pair and self-signed certificate on startup. Useful for development and testing.
  • provideKeystore: Uses an existing PKCS12 keystore provided via a Kubernetes secret. Useful for production.

In 9.0.0, the helper also exposes GET /.well-known/tls.crt and can serve a certificate issued by an external CA (e.g. cert-manager) by mounting the TLS secret as a volume:

did:
  enabled: true
  ingress:
    enabled: true
    className: nginx
    annotations:
      cert-manager.io/issuer: selfsigned-issuer
      cert-manager.io/common-name: did-provider.127.0.0.1.nip.io
      cert-manager.io/private-key-algorithm: ECDSA
    hosts:
      - host: did-provider.127.0.0.1.nip.io
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: ImplementationSpecific
    tls:
      - secretName: did-provider.127.0.0.1.nip.io-tls
        hosts:
          - did-provider.127.0.0.1.nip.io
  volumes:
    - name: certs
      secret:
        secretName: did-provider.127.0.0.1.nip.io-tls
        items:
          - key: tls.crt
            path: tls.crt
  volumeMounts:
    - name: certs
      mountPath: /certs
  config:
    server:
      hostUrl: "https://did-provider.127.0.0.1.nip.io"
      certPath: "/certs/tls.crt"
    generateKey:
      enabled: false

Required action:

Rename did-helper to did in your values file. The top-level didJson section has also been removed — replace it with the did subchart as shown above.

docs.title: TM Forum API: allInOne mode and credentialTypes
docs.text:
Two values have changed:

  • credentialType (string) is now credentialTypes (array)
  • New allInOne mode deploys all TM Forum APIs in a single pod

Required action:

Update your scope configuration: 

# OLD
credentialType: VerifiableCredential

# NEW
credentialTypes:
  - VerifiableCredential

When allInOne.enabled: true, all APIs are served from a single service at tm-forum-api:8080. Update any components that reference individual API services — most notably the marketplace:

marketplace:
  externalApis:
    catalog: http://tm-forum-api-svc:8080
    inventory: http://tm-forum-api-svc:8080
    ordering: http://tm-forum-api-svc:8080
    billing: http://tm-forum-api-svc:8080
    usage: http://tm-forum-api-svc:8080
    party: http://tm-forum-api-svc:8080
    customer: http://tm-forum-api-svc:8080

When allInOne.enabled: false (default), each API retains its own service name and port as before.

docs.title: cert-manager integration
docs.text:
9.x.x adds optional cert-manager support directly as a chart dependency. It can manage TLS certificates for all connector ingresses and replace the previous approach of manually generating and distributing certificates via the helpers/certs scripts (now removed).

Two new values sections are available:

cert-manager — installs cert-manager itself as a subchart (disabled by default):

cert-manager:
  enabled: true
  crds:
    enabled: true   # installs cert-manager CRDs
  startupapicheck:
    enabled: false

certManagerResources — deploys ClusterIssuers after cert-manager is ready (disabled by default):

certManagerResources:
  enabled: true
  namespace: cert-manager   # namespace where cert-manager is deployed
  type: selfsigned          # "selfsigned" or "prod"
  acmeEmail: admins@example.com   # required for "prod" only
  ingressClass: nginx             # required for "prod" only

Two issuer types are supported:

  • selfsigned — creates a self-signed CA and a selfsigned-issuer ClusterIssuer. Suitable for development and internal environments. Does not require external DNS or HTTP challenge resolution.

  • prod — creates a Let's Encrypt production prod-issuer ClusterIssuer using HTTP-01 ACME challenges. Requires a publicly reachable ingress and a valid domain.

Once a ClusterIssuer is available, annotate your ingresses to request certificates automatically. The selfsigned-issuer is already used by did-helper in the example shown in the did-helper section above:

ingress:
  annotations:
    cert-manager.io/issuer: selfsigned-issuer        # for selfsigned
    # cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: prod-issuer    # for Let's Encrypt

Note

certManagerResources uses Helm post-install/post-upgrade hooks to deploy the ClusterIssuers after cert-manager is ready. If you enable both cert-manager and certManagerResources in the same install, the issuers will be created automatically in the correct order.
